#8239. How Joe “Stringbean” McConaughy (Finally) Broke the John Muir Trail FKT

Joe McConaughy thought he would probably start a bit slower than François D’Haene when he went after the Frenchman’s record on the John Muir Trail (JMT) this September. He guessed he’d be maybe 20 or 30 minutes behind in the early miles.

But when McConaughy got to Kearsarge Pass around mile 40, he was an hour off of D’Haene, who ran the Fastest Known Time (FKT) on the 223-mile trail through California’s Sierra Nevada in 2017, just months after winning UTMB for the third time.

“That was definitely a bit of a crack in the armor,” McConaughy told Trail Runner. “But I told myself that maybe he went out at more of a race effort, while my pace was better for a multi-day FKT.”

McConaughy, known by his thru-hiking trail name, “Stringbean,” has more than a few multiday FKTs to his name. He’s set records on the Pacific Crest Trail, Appalachian Trail, Long Trail, and Arizona Trail. And he had two prior record attempts on the JMT, one of which earned him an unsupported FKT.

“I thought my experience could help me beat him,” McConaughy said.

As he chased the ghost of the JMT’s past, McConaughy drew from his many multi-day FKTs and races. All of the miles and mistakes, successes and failures, and lessons and growth along the way helped him ultimately establish a new FKT of 2 days, 16 hours, and 15 seconds, taking nearly three and a half hours off a time that had stood for nearly a decade.

In rock climbing, climbers talk about “flashing” a route. It’s when they successfully climb the whole thing on their first attempt—without any practice or “beta” to help. McConaughy’s JMT effort was pretty much the opposite of flashing. The 35-year-old Seattle-based endurance coach was incredibly familiar with every mile of the JMT. Prior to his record setting attempt this fall, he’d covered the trail four times—the first in 2014—including the two prior FKT attempts. He’d also spent five summers guiding backpacking trips in the Sierra.

So when McConaughy ended up in a blizzard on Muir Pass with snowflakes landing in his eyeballs, it didn’t really stress him out or slow him down. If anything, it helped him move faster as he wanted to get up and over to warmer ground.

“I’ve seen the worst that the Sierra can throw at you,” he said, citing thunderstorms, blizzards, and rugged terrain. “I didn’t have to do a bunch of mental gymnastics, worrying about things I hadn’t experienced before. Instead, I could devote all of my energy to things that actually were issues.”

Most of McConaughy’s issues during the record attempt were ones he expected to occur, was prepared for, and could handle. “The long climbs were long climbs and some of the descents take decades,” he said. But after numerous JMT attempts he knew “it could feel much harder.” A little over a day into his attempt he was two hours ahead of D’Haene’s splits.

The JMT is far from the only goal for which McConaughy’s persistence has paid off. He took seven swings at earning a Golden Ticket into the Western States 100 before clinching one at the Black Canyon 100K on his eighth try in 2025. He’s also raced the Cocodona 250 three times and has a trio of Barkley Marathons starts.

“I like to think I’m more fun than a project-er, but when I look back, that’s pretty much my entire running career,” he said. “I feel like it gives me purpose. I want to do routes that inspire me and motivate me and take what I’ve done wrong, or what I feel like I could improve on, and continue to experiment, tinker, and optimize.”

He’s not as intense as a rock climber going after a seemingly impossible objective like the Dawn Wall, he swears. Rather, it’s about finding the sweet spot where he’s pushing himself to grow but having fun doing it. He’s not training to be the best at any given race or record attempt; he’s training to be the best version of himself for years to come.

“I get a lot of joy from sticking with the process, training with a smile, putting in the work to make a difference, and looking for opportunities to rise like a phoenix and perform the best that I can,”  McConaughy said.

Caroline Himbert, who is coached by McConaughy and set her own unsupported FKT on the JMT this July, helped pace McConaughy on the JMT this fall. “He goes back to things he’s failed at and tries to continuously learn and grow; he loves the science and spreadsheets and takes things seriously,” Himbert said. “But at the same time, he doesn’t take things too seriously and he keeps things fluid and fun.”

As evidenced by the fact that it stood for nine years, the JMT record was stout. D’Haene is known for bringing a newfound level of professionalism to FKT attempts, with a full support staff, set of pacers, and film crew. But rather than seeing the competitive level of the record as a deterrent, McConaughy saw it as part of the draw.

“It’s the granddaddy of FKTs,” he said. “More people have attempted the JMT FKT than pretty much any other premier route that exists—and the fact that François [D’Haene] and Darcy [Piceu] were the [previous] record holders is an ode to the level of attention and competitiveness that it’s gotten.”

On his first attempt in 2022, McConaughy set an unsupported record of three days and one hour. But Jeff Garmire beat it by 13 minutes just 25 days later.

McConaughy knew he could do better, so he tried to reclaim the record in 2024. But he hallucinated in the final miles and wound up off-trail on a class-four scramble, much closer to life-and-limb-threatening risk than he’d anticipated. It was a wake-up call for McConaughy, who always considers what he’s asking of others when he chases a big goal. He’s now the father of a 6-month-old and knew he couldn’t end up in a similar situation—or worse—if he went back.

“That experience made me really rethink what the record meant to me and ask myself if I wanted to do it again,” he said, adding that it felt reckless to go for another unsupported record. But after much reflection, and many conversations with his wife Katie, he decided he had to go back.

“I knew I couldn’t exist as an athlete without trying to put my stamp on the JMT,” he said. “This was my third time [attempting the FKT] on this trail and I wanted to give it my all, and use my best tips and tricks from every other effort to get the record.”

McConaughy showed up with a 12-tab spreadsheet and 12 years of beta to guide his effort this fall. He thought some of the greatest opportunities for improvement lay in fueling, pacing, and recruiting an all-star crew to help him out. In his unsupported-style attempts, he’d had to carry all of his own food and gear with no supply restocks along the way.

At Cocodona in 2025, McConaughy hit a wall that no amount of carbs could fix. He thought he knew how he needed to fuel to compete for the win. He’d done sweat testing and was experimenting with high-carb fueling. But he ended up with GI distress and struggled to breathe. He still finished in a respectable fourth place, but it was far from the finish he wanted.

He started working with nutritionist Meredith Terranova, who suggested he was likely hypernatremic—too high of blood sodium concentration—during Cocodona. He wondered if trying to optimize his performance through a data-driven approach with high carb fueling and sweat tests meant he’d stopped listening to his body.

So on the JMT he turned to real food like trail mix, purees, and waffles, especially on the big climbs—of which there is no shortage with 38,000 feet of elevation gain to cover. He also used recovery drink mixes and fat- and protein-based fuels from his nutrition sponsor, Näak.

“I feel like sticking to more whole food was the biggest learning and the biggest difference maker in my performance,” he said.

He also made up ground through a smarter sleep strategy. In his 2022 attempt, in which he finished six hours behind D’Haene’s record time, McConaughy slept for six hours. He knew there was an opportunity to trim down time spent resting while still sleeping enough to avoid dangerous hallucinations.

He settled on taking a mere 40 minutes of sleep beneath a pine tree on Bear Ridge—around 28 hours in. He thought it might be prudent to get at least an hour but he decided to push it a little with 40 minutes, figuring he could always nap later if he needed it. When he got to his third night out on the trail he was still running strong, cracking jokes, and appreciating his surroundings, Himbert said.

“You could tell he was having a good time and he was a ball of energy,” she said. “I was with him more towards the end, and he was still moving so well. I think that’s the key with this trail; it’s so challenging but if you can still move well towards the end then you can crack these times. I think Joe really nailed it, and it went close to perfect.”

McConaughy’s crew was one of his greatest assets. He learned some things about crewing the JMT after his crew missed him at Kearsarge Pass during his Pacific Crest Trail FKT in 2014. The PCT overlaps with the JMT for about 170 miles. He had to keep going on the PCT for two days with no sleeping bag, only a half-day’s worth of calories, and nothing warmer than a thin windbreaker. “We didn’t really know what we were doing,” he said. Hence the 12-tab spreadsheet this go-around, which was largely for the benefit of his crew and the complicated logistics of supporting a record-attempt on the JMT.

Part of the beauty of the JMT is that it offers an uninterrupted tour of backcountry wilderness. The trail only crosses the road twice over the course of the entire 223 miles. That’s also what makes it a bear to support. Meeting McConaughy on the trail required hiking several miles and thousands of feet of climbing to deliver food and gear. Pacers ran monster sections—usually around 40 miles at a time. But his crew of pacers was up for the challenge, with a collective résumé that boasted JMT FKTs, podium finishes, and 200-mile runs.

“Tara Dower talked about being a vessel on the Appalachian Trail, and I certainly had a similar experience on the JMT,” McConaughy said. “I was able to appreciate the beauty of where I was and the excitement of doing this absurd endurance thing because my crew was always filling my cup instead of making me pour things out to keep going.”

One thing that McConaughy has learned time and time again, is that he runs best when his cup is full.

“Gratitude and joy are the greatest performance-enhancing drugs,” he said.

While he was running, he thought about Katie, who was home solo-parenting so he could acclimatize to the altitude and run for 64 straight hours. He thought about his parents, who enabled him to get outside and run cross-country from a young age. He thought about the people who have supported his running career, and the friends who traveled to the Sierra to help him through the 223-mile journey. And he thought about the Sierra themselves, the mountains that have kept him coming back time and time again for the last 12 years.

“I run my worst when I’m thinking about how far behind someone’s splits I am,” he said. “When I caught myself doing that on the JMT, I thought, ‘This is doing more harm than good. You need to move forward at your own pace, and focus on the things that really matter.’”

After shaving over three hours off such a long-standing record, McConaughy hopes that he’s reached an end with his JMT FKT attempts. With all of the time and effort he has dedicated to the JMT, it feels a bit like a fairytale ending: “The princess was saved,” he said.

Now, he’s ready for a new goal, one he’s ready to chase to fuel his performance and fill his cup

“It’s one of those moments where I realize I’m maybe more capable than I thought I was,” he said. “And that makes it exciting to go back to Cocodona, or Western States, or another FKT, or any number of things to see what I can do.”

#8237. Lone Wolf Custom Gear Crossover Climber Review: The Most Ingenious Climbing Tree Stand Ever Made

The Lone Wolf Custom Gear D'Acquisto Series Crossover Climber is the top choice for mobile hunters who prioritize ultralight portability and dead-quiet performance over comfort. At 11.5 pounds and less than 2 inches wide when packed, it excels for run-and-gun public land deer hunting. Hunters wanting a roomy, comfortable stand or a budget-friendly option should look elsewhere.

I have been testing climbing tree stands for some 30 years now, and in that time, I’ve set up and sat in just about every model made, or at least some version of every base model made. For a long time—probably more than a decade—if you asked me, “What is the best climbing tree stand on the market?” I would have immediately answered, the Lone Wolf Hand Climber.

Ironically, that climber was not the easiest to climb with, and you couldn’t say it was built for comfort, but it was absolutely brilliant in every other way. It weighed nothing, folded down flat as a pizza box, was dead quiet, and bit into the tree like was made of beaver teeth. For run-and-gun—and especially run-and-bow—hunting, there was nothing better.

Well, now there is. The old Hand Climber is no longer produced, and Lone Wolf is now Lone Wolf Custom Gear, or LWCG, but their D’Acquisto Series Crossover Climber is everything the original was, only better. Here’s a close look.

The first thing to understand about the Crossover Climber is that it is uniquely designed for the mobile hunter—for folks who plan to walk far and frequently, often on public land, to get on bucks that other hunters may never know about, and for those who prioritize portability over comfort in a climbing stand.

So, if you’re looking for a cozy climber to scale the same handful of trees on a single property not too far from the truck or ATV—and there’s nothing wrong with that—then don’t waste your money here. There are far-less-expensive climbers that will do that job just fine and, in some ways, better. But if what you want is a climber that you can throw on your back and take anywhere with minimum effort, that accommodates your day pack so you don’t have to stuff your pockets and lash gear, that goes up quick and easy, and whose every detail is purpose-built for your style of hunting—if, in short, you want the absolute state of the art in mobile deer hunting gear, then there is only one climbing stand for you, and you might want start saving your pennies.

The D’Acquisto Crossover Climber is made of machined aluminum with a hammered titanium finish, which makes the stand ultralight and surprisingly quiet, even if you accidentally do bump the metal parts together. Although it is nearly the same size as the old hand climber, it is a full 5 pounds lighter at just 11.5 pounds, and it packs even slimmer.

LWCG kept the original traction belt and cam system for tree attachment, which works great and allows quick adjustments of the seat portion as you climb. Speaking of which, the seat portion now has a recessed, half-moon shape combined with a sliding web seat and removable cushion, an update to the Hand Climber’s rigid seat, which sort of forced you out toward the end of the platform. This new seat system allows you to get closer to the tree, giving you more room to maneuver when standing. The seat portion also adds a micro sit-and-climb bar, which you can use, not use, or remove completely. This is where the “Crossover” name comes from, because whereas Lone Wolf used to sell both Hand Climber and a Sit-and-Climb models, this one offers both options in one unit.

The bottom platform replaces the original’s stabilizing bar with a folding stabilizer that has integrated climbing stirrups, and the whole thing folds down and disappears into the platform for transport. Both the top and bottom portions also have newly designed recessed hinges that fold down perfectly flat. The stabilizing straps that connect the top and bottom portions while climbing have also been updated with metal, instead of plastic, buckles. Finally, there is a new tightening T-bolt that fastens the top and bottom portions together for transport, locking them in place—a huge improvement on the original stand’s bungee cord.

Related: The Complete Guide to Hunting Deer from a Tree Stand

Tree stands aren’t like rifles or binoculars. I can’t report my group-size measurements or scores in a resolution test. What I can tell you is that I have used the stand for a good part of the 2026 bow season so far, and, if you couldn’t tell already, I’m impressed.

The real genius of the Crossover Climber is that everything folds or hinges or meshes or integrates ingeniously to create the most compact and packable (not to mention the lightest) climbing stand on the market. By a mile. As I said, the original Hand Climber packed up as thin as a pizza box. The Crossover packs up as thin as a laptop computer, and the new tightening T-bolt system snugs the two portions of the stand together, so there’s no clinking or clanging while you walk. The stand comes with very good padded shoulder straps, and it is designed so your daypack can attach to and ride along with the stand. The mini sit-and-climb bar even doubles as a support for your pack.

There are a few things I don’t love about this stand. The mesh seat is a bit of a pain. Yes, it slides out of the way to give you more room when standing, which is great, but I found myself having to fiddle with it to reposition for sitting. And I’ll repeat that it is not as roomy or comfortable as many other climbers. You can buy an extension for the bottom platform that adds a few inches, which helps, but this is a small stand. (Personally, I would love it if LWCG came out with a slightly larger version, as I would happily carry a few extra pounds for more room—and it would probably still be lighter than any other climber on the market besides this one.) All of that said, this not a knock on the Crossover, per se, as it is designed to be minimalist. It’s just a fact that you should be aware of before you drop more than a grand on a climbing stand.

Which brings me to the one other thing I don’t love: the price. Oof. Maybe I’m a bad judge, given that I still can’t wrap my head around so many hunters wearing $200 pants. But $1,200 is a price I never thought I’d see on a climbing stand. Of course, I never thought I’d see $8 a pound for beef chuck, either. Everything, it seems, costs three times what it used to. So, I’ll leave it to you to decide if it’s worth it. What I can tell you is no other climbing stand on the market gives half as much attention to detail—details that matter when you’re hunting—as this one. It is brilliantly engineered. And if you’re a mobile hunter who likes a climber, it will be your constant companion and one of your favorite pieces of gear for many deer season’s to come.

#8236. Do Skiers Really Need Another Outerwear Brand? Atomic Thinks So.

Atomic's outerwear features clean lines, minimal logos, and ski-specific details, including articulated construction designed to allow freedom of movement. (Photo: Cam McLeod/Atomic)

The ski world probably doesn’t need another outerwear brand. Dozens of other companies already make quality ski jackets and pants; we’re not exactly short on options.

So when Atomic, the Austrian brand best known for its skis, boots, and bindings, announced it was getting into apparel, I had a pretty obvious question: Why?

At a recent North American launch event I attended at Sundance Mountain Resort in Utah, Atomic acknowledged the challenge of entering an already crowded market. But their answer was simple: After more than 70 years developing ski equipment, who better to make clothing for skiers than a company that lives and breathes skiing?

Fair enough. Though plenty of established apparel companies could make the same argument.

After handling and trying on several pieces from the new collection, including some Gore-Tex Pro outerwear coming next year, I came away impressed. The clothing has clean lines, thoughtful colors, familiar technical materials, and small design details that suggest someone actually thought about what it’s like to spend a day skiing in this stuff.

I haven’t skied in it yet, so the real performance test is still to come. But there’s enough here to make Atomic’s latest expansion worth a closer look. It is a significant expansion, including a complete skiwear collection, from insulated resort jackets and technical shells to bibs, midlayers, base layers, and lifestyle pieces.

Of course, Atomic isn’t the first ski equipment company to see an opportunity in apparel. Salomon, Armada, and Rossignol have all made the move, while Black Diamond, whose roots are in climbing and backcountry skiing, did the same more than a decade ago. Atomic itself has steadily expanded beyond skis, boots, and bindings over the years, adding helmets and goggles to its lineup.

So the move into apparel isn’t entirely surprising. But what does Atomic bring to an already crowded category?

For starters, Atomic isn’t entering the apparel business entirely on its own. The company is part of Amer Sports, which also owns Salomon and Arc’teryx, two brands with decades of experience making technical outerwear. Atomic’s designers explained that they’ve been able to draw on existing fabric research, development resources, and manufacturing expertise within the group.

Atomic also brings its own experience developing ski equipment since 1955. I’ve visited the company’s headquarters in Altenmarkt, Austria and seen firsthand how its engineers develop skis, boots, and bindings, taking prototypes from the office to the snow in minutes and bringing that feedback back into development. Now, outerwear designers follow a similar process, with access to on-snow testing close to headquarters.

Then there’s Atomic’s reputation. In SKI’s 2026 ski test results, Atomic was among the top three most-recognized brands, earning distinctions in categories ranging from backcountry and powder to frontside carving. In my view, that’s a track record worth protecting, and one that gives skiers a reason to take their clothing seriously.

The materials are reassuringly familiar, too. Atomic uses established insulation and fabric technologies from PrimaLoft and Pertex, alongside its own waterproof fabrics. Gore-Tex Pro will join the collection in fall 2027.

For the current lineup, the differences are fairly straightforward. The Revent 2L Insulated Jacket and Pants use Atomic’s 2LAYR Move, a two-layer fabric rated at 20,000 mm waterproofing, with PrimaLoft Silver synthetic insulation for warmth. They’re designed for skiers who prefer an insulated jacket and pants rather than managing multiple layers.

The Revent 3L Jacket and Bib Pants, meanwhile, use Atomic’s 3LAYR Protect, a three-layer fabric also rated at 20,000 mm waterproofing. They’re uninsulated shells, giving skiers more flexibility to add or remove layers as temperatures and conditions change.

Of course, familiar materials and impressive specifications are only a starting point. How a jacket is cut, how the seams are constructed, and how everything fits and moves together can make the difference between loving your gear and being annoyed by it before lunchtime.

And that’s where some of Atomic’s smaller design choices caught my attention.

Atomic describes its approach as performance-first rather than fashion-first, and some of the most interesting details are the ones you might not notice until you’re actually wearing the clothing.

The women’s Snowcloud Puff Jacket is a good example. It has a slightly cropped silhouette, an insulated powder skirt, and a removable hood.

Take the hood off, and there aren’t exposed snaps or awkward attachment points that make it look like something is missing. It’s still a finished-looking jacket.

That matters when you’re using a puffy in different ways. A hood is nice around town or when the jacket is your outermost layer on a dry day. But under a shell that already has a hood, it can feel bulky and unnecessary.

The Revent 2L Shell Anorak, a relaxed, unisex shell, also caught my eye. It has the oversized silhouette and kangaroo pocket you’d expect, but the concealed chest pocket inside the collar was an added touch you don’t often find in anorak styles. As someone who finds it incredibly annoying to put a phone or sunglasses in a kangaroo pocket and have everything bouncing around, I appreciated that.

Other ski-specific details include lift-pass pockets on the left sleeves of most jackets (not just outer shells), helmet-compatible hoods, well-placed ventilation, reinforced pant cuffs, and articulated construction, including pre-shaped elbows and knees designed to accommodate how skiers actually move.

None of these features is revolutionary, of course. But they’re familiar details, executed with the kind of practical attention that matters when you’re spending a full day in ski gear.

As for fit, the pieces I tried generally ran true to size, with a slightly longer, freeride-inspired cut that felt relaxed without being baggy. That said, at six feet tall, I found both pairs of softshell and hardshell pants a little shorter than I’d like.

Atomic’s 2026–’27 apparel collection is available now at Atomic.com. Looking ahead to fall 2027, skiers can expect to find Atomic apparel at select retailers and ski shops as well.

Atomic clearly understands that skiers care about style, too. The aesthetic is clean and understated without being boring. Muted but thoughtful colors, cropped puffies, relaxed anoraks, and monochromatic outfits give the collection plenty of visual appeal. The silhouettes and design details are consistent across categories, so the pieces look like they belong together without requiring a fully matching kit.

But one of my favorite design details is something you might never notice unless you’re a skier, like me, who rolls up your pant cuffs when you’re out of your boots.

On the inside of the right pant cuff, Atomic has hidden its name. That’s the only time the wordmark appears, which feels decidedly cool.

It’s also a pretty good introduction to Atomic’s approach to branding. You won’t find its name prominently displayed across the collection. Instead, the Atomic star appears subtly printed on sleeves or worked into seam placements and color blocking.

The design is recognizable once you know what to look for, but it doesn’t announce itself from across the lift line.

Like Wild Rye and a handful of other ski apparel brands of late, Atomic seems comfortable letting the design speak for itself. There’s something confident about that, especially in a sport where logos can be as loud as the colors they’re printed on.

After all, is there a better compliment than someone saying, “That’s a sick jacket. Who makes it?”

With skis, boots, bindings, helmets, goggles, and now clothing, Atomic can outfit skiers almost completely under one brand.

That doesn’t mean there’s any reason to buy everything from Atomic. Most of us mix and match equipment, developing relationships with different brands for different reasons. Maybe you love your Atomic skis but swear by another company’s boots. Your favorite jacket might come from a brand that doesn’t make hardgoods, and your base layers from somewhere else entirely.

Still, there’s something to be said for gear designed to work together.

Think about wearing a helmet and goggles from the same company. When the fit is seamless, it’s one less thing to worry about.

Atomic seems to be taking a similar approach to its apparel, developing shells, insulation, and base layers with complementary fits, colors, and layering systems. Whether that delivers a meaningful performance advantage remains to be seen, but I understand the intent.

Ultimately, that’s the appeal of well-designed ski equipment, regardless of whose name is on it. We spend enough time and money figuring out what to wear and what to ski. Once we’re on the mountain, we shouldn’t have to think about any of it.

#8235. The World’s Most Cinematic Trail Running Is Hidden Above the Arctic Circle

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Trail Runner’s travel columnist Andy Cochrane has run all over the world, including five trips to the Lofoten Islands above the Arctic Circle in Norway. He shares his hard-earned recommendations on where to run, stay, and eat, what to pack for the unpredictable weather—and how to get there.

As a travel writer, I fly an embarrassing amount. Over three quarters of a million miles in the last decade, or roughly three laps around the Earth each year. That’s a lot of time in a pressurized tube sitting next to strangers, but perhaps a fair price to pay for the privilege of running trails all over the world, from Patagonia to Morocco to Greenland. Picking a favorite destination is difficult, but often actions speak louder than words. I’ve returned to one more than any other: the Lofoten Islands in Norway.

Hidden a hundred miles above the Arctic Circle, Lofoten is best known for its Viking heritage, red fishing  villages, and dramatic coastline—sandy beaches, turquoise waters, and walls of rock that rise 3,000 feet out of the Norwegian Sea. There are very few places in the world where mountains collide with the ocean in such a cinematic way, giving it the best of both worlds—and incredibly unpredictable weather.

On my first trip to the Lofoten Islands in 2017, a snow storm shut down trails in the alpine, so I explored the lowlands, dabbled in fishing and kayaking, and enjoyed a nightly sauna. Since then I’ve returned four times to explore different corners of the islands and am planning to go back again next year, because there is still so much to explore, especially if you love empty trails and technical running. Here’s why I think Lofoten could be the next great trail destination and how you can visit before it gets too crowded.

The Lofoten Islands are an archipelago in northern Norway that stretch from the mainland into the North Atlantic. At 68 degrees 54 minutes north latitude, they sit further north than most communities in Greenland and all but a dozen or so towns at the top of Alaska. The chain consists of five main islands and hundreds of smaller ones, connected by bridges and underwater tunnels. (Oh, the joys of Norwegian infrastructure!)

Combined, the islands cover a total of 474 square miles, roughly the size of the city of Los Angeles. However, they are home to just 25,000 full-time residents, most of whom live in Svolvær and Leknes. Suffice to say, the interior is remote and rugged; it’s common to find yourself on a trail without a single human in sight, despite the lack of trees and views in all directions.

Although there are offshore oil reserves nearby, drilling is prohibited in Lofoten (unlike much of Norway), which has allowed cod fishing and tourism to flourish. The landscape is a mix of granite spines and tussocked tundra, with a few birch and mountain ash stands sprinkled in. When storms roll in—which they do often—there is very little protection, which can be a humbling experience.

The trail network in Lofoten is a patchwork of everything from unmaintained user trails to heavily engineered routes like Reinebringen’s 1,978 stone steps. As a whole they skew towards the technical end of the spectrum; most are steep, rocky, and stout. It’s common to gain a thousand feet per mile or more.

The vast majority of trails start near sea level and ascend through bogs and brush, climbing into the alpine via scree fields and off-camber granite slabs. Expect your shoes to get muddy and shirt to be saturated in sweat as you climb to the summit. Some marshes have wooden planks and some ridgelines have cairns, but they aren’t guaranteed. It’s best to always bring a good map and a better attitude.

While there isn’t an official count of trails on the islands, a good estimate is around 150, including everything from short beach hikes to high ridge lines. For ambitious trail runners, the Lofoten Crossing is an unofficial 100-mile thru-route from Delp to Å, and uses a mix of local paths, beaches, and roads. It’s a great way to see the entire chain of islands, even if it skips some of the serene trails. A few of my other favorites are the steep climb up to Himmeltindan (2,700 feet in 2.1 miles), crossing the interior of Vestvågøya from Leknes to the eastern end, and almost any of the remote trails at the end of the archipelago near Å, many of which reside inside Lofotodeen National Park.

Lofoten sees over a million tourists each year, heavily focused on the summer months. The crowds get so bad in July and August that iconic trails like Ryten, Fløya, and Mannen are probably not worth visiting. In the spring and fall Lofoten becomes a lot more enjoyable, because it offers more solitude on the trails, open spots at restaurants, and generally friendlier locals. I have a slight preference for the fall, mostly because I reserve most of the spring for skiing, which also is pretty great in Lofoten.

It’s also worth considering the weather and daylight. For about a month from early December to early January, the sun doesn’t rise above the horizon. Days lengthen dramatically in the spring, from 6 hours in February to over 18 by the end of April. The Midnight sun rises in late May and sets in mid-July, offering 24 hours of daylight for a month and a half straight. Almost too much!

Weather is fickle all year but especially in the spring and fall, as temps float in the 40s and 50s Fahrenheit. Snow usually melts in May and the mountains undergo a rapid transition to green. In the fall the foliage turns to a golden and red mix, storms begin to batter the coast, and the Northern Lights illuminate the night sky as early as September. Thankfully saunas are common and help make cold weather running more enjoyable.

Getting to Lofoten takes more time than most destinations in Europe. The drive from Oslo is around 20 hours and the combination of train and ferry takes even longer. The fastest way to get to the islands is a flight to Bodø and then a puddle hop prop plane to Svolvær or Leknes. This saves time and helps avoid weather-dependent ferries, but is often more expensive.

I prefer to fly from Oslo to Narvik, which sits on the mainland adjacent to the islands, and rent a car. The drive takes between 2-4 hours, depending on where I’m staying, but is always worth it for the views. Plus, public transit is limited in Lofoten, so having a car allows me to get to quieter places. For example, the cinnamon rolls at Unstad are to die for—but the only way to get there is to drive (or go on a 80-mile round-trip bike ride).

Traditional fishing lodges, called rorbuer, are built on poles over the water. Many have been converted to cozy places to stay. My favorite is Hattvika Lodge in the town of Ballstad. The restaurant next door, Fangst, is one of the best in the area. For those wanting to stay further off the beaten path, Nusfjord would be a great option. For a wider selection of restaurants, consider a stay in Svolvær or Leknes. Regardless, it’s important to book early, because the best places fill up months in advance.

If someone told me the Offtrail Ultra was designed specifically for Lofoten, I wouldn’t blink an eye. The 5 mm lugs are perfect in mud and scree, the toe grip is great on granite slaps, the integrated gaiter keeps out debris, and the midsole is stable enough for the dynamic movements necessary in this terrain. Hard to imagine a better fit, honestly.

Designed for cold and wet weather, the Run Cold wool socks are designed with high-impact wear zones to help them last longer, but don’t feel overbuilt at all. Instead they are stretchy and comfortable, with a seamless toe to reduce chafing. They work well with tights and running pants, which I use in spring and fall running in cold climates like Lofoten.

Over the last few years I’ve trended towards running belts, but I make an exception for a place like Lofoten, where you want to bring a few extra things. The Triack has a snug fit with almost no bounce thanks to a bungee system that’s easy to adjust on the fly. Plus, with four easy-access pockets, I can carry spare layers, gloves, snacks, water, camera, and first aid easily.

The name is a bit of a misnomer, because it’s actually made of merino wool. The wool helps regulate temperature better than other materials, keeping you warmer at the start and cooler when you heat up, not to mention not smelling after days of use. I love the hood and neck gaiter for colder days, and how the hoodie works great under a raincoat, too.

#8233. Hike of the Week: Explore a Wilderness With Wolves and Endless Flat-Topped Peaks

The Flat Tops Wilderness Area in northwestern Colorado is one of my favorite places to drop off-grid. Among its basalt peaks and sweeping valleys are some of the state’s best trails, in my opinion. Its “hidden-gem” days are long gone—lots of people, especially those from Colorado’s Western Slope, recreate here. Yet, you can still find areas where you’re the only human for miles.

That solitude can be intoxicating. The 10.9-mile out-and-back to Marvine Lakes via the Marvine Trail could easily be a dayhike. But when I visited with a group of friends this summer, we wanted to spend time marinating in the scenery, lounging on the lakes’ shoreline with some beers, and enjoying a nice bagged meal with friends. I saw more wildlife on that trip than I have on any other in a long time: We crossed paths with elk, mule deer, beavers, and a silver-colored canid that looked much bigger than any coyote I’ve ever seen. Was it a wolf? I can’t say with certainty, but the Flat Tops is one of the areas where Colorado’s wolf reintroduction program has been most successful.

The trail starts at East Marvine Campground, about 35 miles east of Meeker. When we arrived, several outfitters were saddling horses and preparing to ride out with their groups. The trail is multi-use, though mountain bikes and motorized vehicles are not permitted in wilderness areas. Dogs are allowed, and leashes are not required. But hikers should stay both stay horse- and bear-aware.

The hike itself isn’t too strenuous, climbing just 1,045 feet over the 5.4 miles to the lakes. It passes small beaver ponds, pops out into meadows where you might catch a glimpse of browsing elk or deer, and winds through thick old-growth pine and spruce forest. The hike follows pristine Marvine Creek the entire way. Water is never an issue as long as you’ve got a means of purifying it.

When you arrive at lower Marvine Lake, you’ll find turquoise water reflecting the stratigraphy of the towering cliffs that hem the valley. The trail splits and goes around both sides of the lake, passing dispersed camping spots. We picked one on the very far end of lower Marvine Lake, between it and upper Marvine Lake. Our group hung out well past dark, expecting the kind of stars that only the remote corners of the Rockies can deliver. We were not disappointed.

We hiked out the next day, retracing our footsteps to the trailhead. If you wanted a longer hike, the Marvine Trail extends deeper east into the Flat Tops Wilderness Area and connects to an entire trail network. Following it all the way out to Twin Lakes and returning via the East Marvine Lakes Trail would make a 22.5-mile loop and end at the same trailhead you started at, with more alpine ponds and lakes along the way.

#8232. The Best Trail Running Shoes for Fall 2026

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

The best trail running shoes boost our confidence on singletrack to scree fields, sand to slick rock. They’re comfortable and nimble and help us run fast or forever, depending on the adventure. As the days grow shorter and colder we’re also looking for shoes that excel under a wide variety of circumstances, like wet leaves, rime ice, and snow. And as the weather deteriorates, we’re also leaning more on road-to-trail models for the days when the roads and paths are calling our names.

Over two to four months of testing on varied terrain across Santa Barbara to Boulder and Nebraska to New Hampshire, our testers Lisa Jhung, Cory Smith, Johnathan Beverly, and Abby Levene provided detailed feedback on fit, comfort, speed, traction, cushioning, and their joy of running. The result is Trail Runner Magazine’s best trail shoes for fall 2026. Considering that the “best” shoe can run differently on someone else’s feet, our review is specially curated with a shoe claiming the title of each chosen category it achieves best. For even more models, check out Outside’s guide to best trail running shoes for fall.

Weight: 7.5 ounces (men’s 8.5), 6.2 ounces (women’s 8) Stack Height: 28.5–21.5 mm Drop: 7 mm Sizing: 7-12.5, 13, 14, 15 (men’s), 6-11 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Responsive and springy + Weightless feeling underfoot + Good ground feel + Excellent traction – Runs small (go half a size up) –Expensive

If the Norda 005 was a car, it would be the Mercedes AMG E63S Wagon. That is to say: it’s quiet performance luxury. IYKYK, as the kids say. Coming in at just 214 grams (7.5 ounces) for a men’s U.S. 8.5, it’s one of the lightest trail running shoes on the market. It’s also made from the highest quality materials: A Biodyneema upper makes it both durable and highly breathable. A slick of Vibram “Megagrip Elite” rubber renders the outsole ultra tacky on the trails while rolling over the roads. And, perhaps most importantly, the midsole is made completely from a proprietary Mouse Arnitel TPEE—a supercritical foam generally only used in small amounts because of the cost—making the shoe featherlight, energetic, and highly durable.

And the simplicity of the design lets the quality shine. As such, it’s a light, fast trail running shoe that can do it all. We’d turn to this shoe for anything from easy days on mixed surfaces, to “fast” trail 100-milers like Western States or Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc. Trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene wore one pair of the Norda 005 for the Tour du Mont Blanc, a five-day, 110-mile adventure through the Alps, and she didn’t think about her feet once. There is no higher praise.

The midsole is tuned to be slightly firmer than the superfoam in road racers and thus provides an energetic, bouncy ride that doesn’t trampoline you in wild directions off the trail. While the lack of a plate may disqualify the Norda 005 from being a true trail “super shoe,” don’t mistake semantics for inferiority. We didn’t miss a carbon plate here, and its absence allows for enhanced ground feel and adaptability to varied terrain. The foam and rocker deliver a smooth roll and plenty of precision.

The only real downside to this shoe is the price tag. But sometimes, you get what you pay for. Read our full review of the Norda 005.

Weight: 9.5 oz (men’s), 8.4 oz (women’s) Stack Height: 32–28 mm Drop: 4 mm Sizing: 7-13, 14, 15 (men’s), 5-12 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Excellent traction + Lightweight and nimble – Slippery laces require double-knotting

We’ve tested every version of the Saucony Peregrine since the model’s debut in 2011, and this sixteenth iteration just might be our all-time favorite. The shoe has long been capable of making us feel nimble on rugged terrain, with its great balance of ground feel and cushioning, plus traction on all kinds of trail, wrapped up in a lightweight package. But version 16 takes the Peregrine’s trail capabilities to new levels, and at $150, it’s an easy pick for Best Value.

The upgraded Vibram Megagrip outsole grips rock slabs with aplomb, while the four-millimeter lugs dig into loose dirt and soft ground (though some sandy-trail testers craved even deeper, toothier lugs). The balanced midsole—not too springy, not too mushy, not too thick—delivers a strong connection to the trail while still feeling responsive and shock absorbing, even during wild descents. The flexible, breathable mesh upper with added toe protection kept out trail debris and warded off snags from roots and branches.

The fit of this trail running shoe somehow made a variety of testers feel like it was custom-made for them. It locks down the heel, and the just-roomy-enough toebox allowed toe space to breathe while maintaining control. “The fit is just perfect,” said a tester. “I feel secure and supported from heel to toe, and side to side.”

The Salomon Genesis 2 earned mountain-goat status among our crew, providing outstanding traction over loose dirt and rock. Its supportive Matryx upper—constructed with thin, high-tenacity yarns and durable Kevlar—secures narrow and wide feet alike via Salomon’s quick-pull lacing system. The forefoot offers slightly more room than version 1, enhancing overall comfort without sacrificing agility.

The outsole, made of Salomon’s Contagrip rubber with toothy, 4 mm lugs, provided excellent traction on all surfaces, giving us confidence, even on scrambles over large rocky slabs and slippery descents.

Pros and Cons + Extremely versatile + Comfortable for all-day wear – Traction could be better

The Nike Trail Pegasus 5 has been our top choice for road-to-trail runs for several seasons, so we were concerned that its newly branded replacement, the Nike ACG Pegasus Trail, would mess with its winning formula. But as soon as we stepped into the new model, we breathed a sigh of relief. The shoe is just as comfortable as its predecessor and, after testing, has proven to be just as capable on and off roads and over gravel, continuing its reign as the most versatile shoe in this roundup.

The midsole foam—Nike’s injection-molded ReactX—feels responsive and cushions comfortably on concrete, pavement, and hard-packed dirt. The outsole traction, from 3.5 mm lugs made of the brand’s proprietary “All Terrain Compound 2.0,” is tackier on wet terrain than the previous version, but still pales in comparison to Vibram MegaGrip.

What makes this shoe work from roads to singletrack trails is the fit and foothold. Even our most narrow-footed testers felt a secure hold without any pressure points, which allows precise footing on trails, no matter how steep or rocky. This shoe’s versatility makes it a great pick as a one-trick pony for the casual runner who doesn’t need a lighter, faster race shoe, and a solid choice for travel.

Weight: 9.5 oz (unisex) Stack Height: 40–34 mm Drop: 6 mm Sizing: 5-12,13 (men’s), 6.5-13.5, 14.5 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Extremely lightweight for a 40 mm stack + Great stability – Premium pricetag

Brooks has a reputation for building a great shoe and sticking to that formula, giving loyal fans a consistent ride, model after model. The tradeoff? It can make the brand seem boring. The all-new Brooks Cascadia Elite shatters that mold. It’s one of the most exciting shoes Brooks has launched in years, and arguably one of the most exciting trail releases of the year.

Despite sharing a name, the Cascadia Elite is nothing like the everyday, cushioned Cascadia trail runner: It’s a trail racing super shoe that is lighter, faster, and more nimble. The standout feature is the 100% PEBA midsole paired with a carbon-infused PEBAX plate that strikes a perfect balance between a springy and stable ride. On smooth, flowy single track in Santa Barbara, CA, running in the Cascadia Elite felt almost effortless, and a ton of fun.

40 millimeters under the heel is a lot of foam to deal with, but the ride never felt squishy or overly bouncy in off-camber footing. A wide platform, paired with a flexible, embedded horseshoe-shaped plate, keeps the Cascadia Elite from being tippy. That width does come at a cost, though; picking tight lines through technical terrain requires precise footing to keep from getting wedged between rocks.

If you’re in the market for a trail running shoe, first consider the type of trails you run on regularly: do you tackle rugged, mountainous terrain, or stick to mellow dirt paths? Some trail shoes can handle both adequately, while others are specialized and excel in one or the other. Shoes with smaller lugs are generally better on smoother, firmer terrain, whereas shoes with deeper, more aggressive outsoles are optimized for steep, muddy, or rocky trails. If you like to feel the trail and dance around rocks and roots, you’ll likely prefer a light, more minimal shoe, but if you’d rather let the shoe roll over trail variations, cushioning and protecting while you zone out, you should look for a shoe with a thicker midsole.

Once you’ve narrowed the search to a certain type of trail shoe, you need to find a pair that complements your unique body and stride. Every runner’s body, gait, speed, experience, and ride preferences are different, so every runner will interact differently with each trail shoe. The shoe that your best friend or your sister-in-law loves may be uncomfortable for you and make running feel slow, sluggish, or even painful. Finding the perfect pair of trail running shoes is a seriously personal affair.

The process for choosing the best running shoes is a matter of finding the models that both fit your foot and also feel best when you’re running. To determine fit and feel, there’s no substitute for trying the shoes on and running in them.

When assessing fit, first pay attention to length. You need room at the end of your toes as your feet lengthen during their dynamic movements on the run. A rule of thumb is to allow a thumb’s width between your longest toe and the end of the shoe. Runners often wear a running shoe a half or full size bigger than their street shoes.

Ensure that the shape of the sole and the upper matches your foot shape. The sole should be as wide or wider than your foot for the whole length, and match the curve of your arch comfortably. The shoe should hold your foot securely over the instep, while allowing the ball of the foot and the toes to splay and flex when you roll forward onto them. Your heel shouldn’t slip when you lift it, and the arch should be able to dome and lengthen naturally. Nothing should bind or rub as you roll through the stride.

If the shoe fits, it’s time to take them on a short run on a treadmill, around the store, or, ideally, down the block and back. Every trail running shoe has a unique ride created by the type and density of foam in the midsole and the geometry of that foam: its thickness, width, heel-to-toe drop, molded sidewalls or flares, and forefoot flexibility or rocker shape (plus, in an increasing number of models, the presence of and type of embedded plate). Each of these elements interact with each other and your stride to determine how the shoe reacts on landing, how much it cushions, how stably it supports, how smoothly it transitions from landing to toe off, and how quickly and powerfully it rebounds.

The best way to choose trail running shoes that complement your body and stride is to find the ones that feel right on the run. Benno Nigg, the world-leading biomechanics professor who proposed this method of shoe selection, calls it the “comfort filter,” but makes clear it is far more than how plush the shoe feels when you step into it. What you want to assess is whether the shoe allows and supports the way your feet want to move, what Nigg calls your “preferred movement path.” In the right shoe, while running at your normal pace, you will touch down where you expect to land, roll smoothly and stably through the stride without noticing the shoe, feel both cushioned from and connected to the ground, and push off naturally, quickly, and powerfully. When this comes together you’ll know that you’ve found your pair.

It’s likely that several shoes will feel good on your feet. To find the most comfortable, it helps to compare them back to back, like an eye doctor will do with corrective lenses: flipping between “A” or “B,” “1” or “2.” You may also find that different shoes feel better at different paces or level of fatigue, and you may want more than one pair. In fact, research shows that wearing a variety of different shoes is one of the few proven ways to reduce injury risk as it appears to vary the stresses on your feet and joints.

Running shoes have long been marketed and sold as prescriptive devices to help runners stay healthy, but there is little scientific evidence correlating shoes, or any specific shoe properties—like cushioning or pronation control—with running injuries. Medical professionals say that it is highly difficult to determine whether a runner needs a certain type of shoe, and studies have shown that prescribing shoes using traditional methods like treadmill gait analyses or wet-foot arch height tests don’t consistently reduce injuries.

Don’t assume that you need more cushioning or more stability if you have sore joints, or if you’re a heavier runner, or if you’re a beginner—evidence doesn’t support many common beliefs. The best way prevent injury is find two or three different pairs that feel right on the run, ease into using them, and vary your shoes, your running surface and your pace regularly (plus avoid rapid increases in your training load and work on improving your mechanics).

Each season, we evaluate new releases from top outdoor brands, distributing samples to testers based on foot shape and local trail conditions and preferences. For this fall update, we evaluated 5 new models alongside 91 previously tested shoes to select the best trail running shoes on the market.

Over two to four months of testing on varied terrain across the country (from Santa Barbara to Boulder, Nebraska to New Hampshire), our team provided detailed feedback on fit, comfort, traction, cushioning, and responsiveness. We combined these reports with our own trail testing to select category winners and top recommendations for every type of runner.

Freelance journalist, editor, and author Lisa Jhung has researched, tested, and written about running shoes for the past decade and a half, much of that time for Outside. She coordinates a fleet of female shoe testers out of Boulder, Colorado, and says her home office is a perpetual obstacle course of cardboard boxes and piles of running shoes. Lisa’s written about gear of all kinds for numerous national magazines as both an editor and freelancer, including a stint as the shoes and gear blogger and trail running microsite editor for Runner’s World.

A high school jumper and occasional sprinter/hurdler, she started running—really running—after walking off the collegiate volleyball team, and moved on to road and trail races of any distance, triathlons, adventure races, and mountain running. She’s happiest testing rugged trail shoes on gnarly terrain, and also loves a good neighborhood jaunt…but is almost always looking for ribbons of dirt. Lisa is the author of Running That Doesn’t Suck: How to Love Running (Even if You Think You Hate It) and Trailhead: The Dirt on All Things Trail Running.

Cory’s passion for running started over 30 years ago in high school when he became the number six ranked runner in the nation at 3000 meters his senior year. After high school, he competed at Villanova University, earning two NCAA Division I Championship showings. Today, he’s determined not to let age slow him down and competes on the national master’s circuit, running a 4:12 (4:30 mile pace) 1500 meters and 9:04 (4:52 mile pace) 3000 meters in 2021 at age 43. He prefers a hard track workout or tempo run over an easy long run any day but also appreciates a challenging trail or mountain run.

His obsession with running shoes started in 2014 when he wrote his first shoe review for Gear Institute. Since then, he’s tested and reviewed hundreds of running shoes, clothing, and gear for Outside, Runner’s World, Footwear News, and other outlets. He has a soft spot for speedy shoes over heavy trainers but loves dissecting all shoes equally and thinking like a product engineer to explain the why behind every design detail. Cory is the Founder of Run Your Personal Best, an online running coaching business, and since its inception in 2014, has coached runners to over 100 Boston Marathon Qualifying times.

Jonathan fell in love with running his freshman year of high school and quickly became fascinated with finding the perfect pair of running shoes. That quest got a boost when he became editor of Running Times in 2000 and started receiving every new model as they were released. The parade of shoes continued while he served as shoe editor for Runner’s World, then editor of PodiumRunner, and currently fitness gear editor at Outside. Having now worn nearly every running shoe created in this century—and a fair amount of those dating back to the early models of the ’70s—he’s given up on finding the one best and now relishes the wide variety of excellent options.

Once a 2:46 marathoner regularly doing 50+ mile weeks, recent injuries and his age have reduced his volume and slowed his pace—but he still enjoys an uptempo workout or two each week. #8230. Great Hydration is About More than Just Electrolytes

Harmless Harvest shelf-stable coconut water. (Photo: Harmless Harvest)

Hydration comes up a lot when we talk about performance and recovery. Are you drinking enough water? Are you getting enough electrolytes? Are you tracking your fluid intake? It can be overwhelming to keep tabs of every statistic and ounce, but the hype around hydration isn’t without cause. Hydration is not only an essential component of pre-, mid- and post-workout performance. It’s an essential part of everyday life.

Electrolytes are a particular point of focus among performance athletes. Electrolytes are the minerals that help maintain the balance of fluids inside and outside your body’s cells. This is a critical consideration when it comes to high-exertion workouts where you’re losing lots of fluids through sweat.

The market is more saturated (pun intended) than ever with tablets, powders and pouches galore to help you optimize and maximize your electrolyte intake. But hydration doesn’t have to be as complicated as all that—and the conversation surrounding electrolytes doesn’t have to be reserved for elite athletes. It can be an everyday consideration for your morning walk, a quick out-and-back hike, or your daily commute to the office. And it all starts with a single coconut.

That’s the mission behind Harmless Harvest, a California-based company championing the coconut, turning a remarkable fruit into a remarkable lineup of products. It’s new pantry-friendly coconut water contains one ingredient: 100% coconut water with no added sugar or preservatives. The simplicity of their products ladder up to the simplicity of the brand’s philosophy—that great taste, quality ingredients, and premium tasting hydration should be for everyone to enjoy. Uncomplicated hydration doesn’t have to be a statistic for you to overanalyze—it can be an intentional and enjoyable part of your everyday life.

So what’s so great about a simple bottle of coconut water? Well, it’s just that: the simplicity. All on its own, coconut water delivers naturally occurring electrolytes, including potassium, to support everyday hydration. Unlike the formulated hydration drinks, tablets and powders that rely on added electrolytes, coconut water provides those muscle-supporting, fluid-balancing minerals into every bottle of Harmless Harvest coconut water naturally. Every bottle is made with a single ingredient with that naturally sweet coconut taste that’s completely delicious and refreshing.

From your pantry to wherever the day takes you, Harmless Harvest’s newest coconut water makes it easier than ever to keep great-tasting hydration close at hand. With no refrigeration required, you can keep bottles at room temperature until you’re ready to enjoy. Grab a bottle on the way to yoga, before a big day on the slopes, or just on the way to work. And unlike the traditional flash pasteurization commonly used by beverage producers, Harmless Harvest’s optimized heat treatment and micro-filtration preserves the fruit’s natural sweetness and nutrients, so you’re getting everything the mighty coconut has to offer.

Another question you might be asking is why is Harmless Harvest’s coconut water pink? Rather than using additives to control color variation from bottle to bottle, the company has embraced the pink hue that can come with the interaction between the coconut water’s antioxidants and natural elements like light and temperature.

Harmless Harvest’s commitment to sustainability and environmentally conscious practices extends beyond the bottle, too. The brand works with coconut growers in Thailand to source ethically farmed, non-GMO coconuts and also invests in initiatives that support farmers and their communities. These conscientious business practices aim to bring you products that you can sip with peace of mind.

Coconut water may not be the first thing you think to grab before a big workout or after a long run. It’s not a product that we typically associate with performance and recovery, but perhaps that’s the whole point. Don’t get us wrong, electrolytes are important, but in the age of optimization, where every mile, calorie and ounce of water is tracked, logged, and analyzed, it’s good to get back to the basics.

Being well-hydrated shouldn’t be reserved for when you’re pushing your body to its limits. Harmless Harvest’s mission is to show that just like general wellness, proper hydration goes beyond a numerical value—it’s about being mindful and listening to your body, one sip at a time.

#8229. The Rules of Trail Running Etiquette, from the ATRA President

As the president of the American Trail Running Association (ATRA)—a title that sounds more impressive than it is—and co-author of The Ultimate Guide to Trail Running,” which is now in its third edition, I know a little about the proper behavior of trail runners. And as a six-decade trail veteran myself, I also know a little about the improper behavior of trail runners.

To me, the “rules” of trail running are quite simple and boil down to two principles: respect nature, and respect other users.

Those two tenets blossom into about 10 “strong suggestions” for sustainable, copasetic trail experiences, but, like with the Golden Rule, it all comes down to showing respect. Here are the basics of what you should know when you hit the trails:

Close any gates you open, don’t disturb the wildlife or livestock, and respect private land and get permission to enter.

Take only photos and pack out at least as much as you brought in, including gel wrappers. If needed, wear shorts, a jacket, or hydration pack with zip pockets to stow rubbish found on the trail.

Don’t disturb wildlife as frightened animals may be dangerous. Steer clear of trails that disturb sensitive habitats during nesting or mating seasons. When passing horses, use special care and follow directions from the horseback riders. Consider turning around and going another direction when faced with large herds of animals.

Don’t play your music loudly, engage in boisterous conversations with your fellow runners (or through speakerphone), or listen to headphones so loudly that you are unaware of your surroundings. Along the same lines, do your social media influencing elsewhere. Nature is not your recording studio. We don’t want to hear you, and you ought to be able to hear others.

We expect the same of cyclists. This should be obvious but, then again, all of this should be.

As trail runners, we move relatively quickly, especially when we seemingly emerge from nowhere on unsuspecting trail users. This may be alarming, so anticipate and give a courteous and audible announcement of your presence and intention to pass hikers on the trail by stating something along the lines of, “On your left,” or “Trail,” as you approach. Keep an eye out for those wearing headphones, as they won’t hear your warning. Be courteous when passing, slowing down or stopping if necessary to prevent accidental contact. Be ready to yield to all other trail users (cyclists, hikers, horses) even if you have the posted right of way.

This is likely to be controversial, but consider not bringing your dog on group runs and, when you do run with your dogs, be sure to leash them and keep them under your control when necessary to prevent any wildlife disturbances. Be sure to pack out their (and your) waste.

Be cognizant that off-leash dogs often chase wildlife and degrade the outdoor experience of other trail users.

Greet and say “Excuse me” to those you see and pass on the trail. This should be a common practice if for no other reason than to alert others to your presence and not frighten anyone. Similarly, be sure to stay in control of your speed, especially when you could cause rocks or other trail features to fall.

If you startle someone, apologize, and thank them if they’ve stepped aside. A little kindness goes a long way on the trail.

Don’t cut the switchbacks or widen trails by running around puddles,downed trees, or when it is too muddy

Don’t create your own trails by running off preexisting, well-marked trails. When multiple trails exist, run on the most worn. Stay off closed trails and obey all postings.

Run single file in the middle of a trail, even if it’s laden with a fresh blanket of snow or thick mud. Go over, not around, obstacles like puddles,rocks, or downed tree limbs, as that widens trails, damages vegetation, and causes unnecessary erosion.

In other words, participate in trail maintenance and give back to the trail community.

In a now-infamous Outside opinion piece of seven years ago that went viral, Marc Peruzzi claimed that trail runners are lazy parasites. Ultrarunner and lawyer Stephanie Case wrote a response piece, saying more could be done, agreeing with my stance that “we are guilty as charged … we need [to do] more. A lot more.” Case continued, “Indeed, as trail running continues to increase in popularity, it will become even more important that we expand our volunteer and conservation efforts.”

So, carry your weight and do trail work. Volunteer. Go plogging on your local trails.

Technically, those ascending are supposed to have the right of way but, in practice, people often yield to descenders, likely due to speed and momentum. Be polite, maintain control, and be prepared to yield to other users, including horseback riders.

Split larger groups into smaller groups as bigger numbers can intimidate other users and have a greater environmental impact on trails.

If you come across someone in distress, stop and check whether they need help.

Don’t become a liability by taking risks, getting lost, or ignoring trail closures that require dangerous rescues. Carry proper clothing, nutrition, and hydration so as not to put yourself at risk of exposure. Safety first is always a good rule.

If running alone, familiarize yourself with the area where you plan to run and let at least one other person know your intended route. Be prepared for the weather and conditions when you start your run and plan for the worst, given the likely duration of your run. Know and respect your limits and report unsafe conditions and activities to the proper authorities.

Trail running is beautifully simple. So is being a courteous trail runner. Follow these tips for proper etiquette and keep the trails safe, welcoming, and wild!
