#8227. How a 20-Year-Old Texas Climber Lost His Life on the Matterhorn

Kieran Liner, a 20-year-old climber based in Austin, TX, died in an accident on the Matterhorn in October. (Photo: Courtesy Precenia Newman)

A 20-year-old climber named Kieran Liner from Austin, Texas, died on October 27 after falling from the Matterhorn’s Hörnli Ridge. He was climbing with his friend Eli Hawkins.

Valais Cantonal Police said the two climbers were ascending shortly after 6 a.m. when rocks fell near them at about 11,500 feet. Hawkins lost sight of Liner and immediately called for help. An Air Zermatt helicopter responded. Rescuers found Liner below the route and pronounced him dead at the scene.

Prosecutors opened an investigation to determine the precise circumstances of the fall. The initial police statement reported rockfall nearby, but didn’t specify exactly how Liner fell or died.

Hawkins, who says he met Liner in Austin around five years ago, called him his “best bud” and his climbing partner. “It is what it is,” Hawkins told Climbing. “He died doing what he loved.”

Originally from Pensacola, Florida, Liner had lived in Austin since 2020. According to Hawkins, Liner liked Modest Mouse, IPAs, and American Spirit Blues. But what he loved most, Hawkins wrote, was climbing in the mountains.

In an obituary shared last week, Liner’s sister Precenia Newman remembered her younger brother as a skateboarder, golfer, and alpinist—someone who brought the same enthusiasm to everything he pursued. “He approached everything in life with 150% of himself,” Newman wrote.

Newman described a close circle of friends who had become family through shared adventures and everyday life. Among them was Hawkins, whose friendship and life as Liner’s roommate she singled out as especially meaningful. She also remembered the love surrounding Liner from his parents, Justine Hamel and Nick Liner, as well as his siblings, grandparents, aunts, uncles, nieces, and nephews. Newman has organized a fundraiser to bring him home so the family can celebrate his life in Pensacola and Austin.

While Hawkins grew up climbing as a kid with his father and uncle, Liner got into the sport later in life, but it quickly became his passion. Hawkins said the two of them had strong mentors, including Hawkins’s dad Stephen, Ben Darce, and his uncle Bryan Hawkins who owns a climbing gym in Everett, Washington. “He was fearless,” Hawkins said of Liner. “I was fearless—still am. I’m going to keep climbing for him. We just climbed hard and partied hard.”

This past July, Liner had started an Instagram account called @mountkieran dedicated primarily to climbing and mountaineering content. His first reel captured climbing Mt. Rainier. Most of his content leaned humorous, with jokes about “Conrad Anger” and poking fun at himself as an “Austin influencer” while board climbing.

But occasionally, Liner shared more serious content, like footage of ascending a steep snow pitch with a quote from Reinhold Messner: “To go on an adventure, you need difficulties, you need danger. If death were not a possibility, coming out would be nothing.”

Generally considered the most popular and easiest route by which to ascend the Matterhorn, the Hörnli Ridge rises roughly 4,000 vertical feet from the Hörnli Hut to the 14,692-foot summit. Rated AD (“fairly difficult”) on the alpine scale, the route combines sustained exposed scrambling with technical rock climbing rated around 5.4. In general, parties take four to five hours for the ascent, plus another five to six hours for the descent, which involves downclimbing and rappelling much of the same terrain.

Fixed ropes assist climbers on certain sections, but parties also bring their own ropes. Snow and ice can be encountered near the summit, requiring crampons and an ice axe. The technical grade captures only part of the challenge of navigating and descending that exposed terrain in mountaineering boots.

To learn more about the Hörnli Ridge where Liner’s accident took place, I reached out to my friend Steph Abegg, who claimed the fastest known time by a woman on the route this past summer.

In 1985, Abegg’s dad soloed the Matterhorn in a T-shirt. Twenty years later, when Abegg and her sister were in Zermatt and decided to climb it, that was the image they held in their minds. Their dad was an experienced climber, and he’d enjoyed ideal conditions on his ascent.

Accordingly, the Abegg sisters expected a casual adventure. Instead, they encountered verglas—a thin glaze of ice on the rock—and a whiteout. They turned around at the Solvay Hut, an emergency shelter at 13,133 feet. At this point, they were roughly 2,440 vertical feet above the Hörnli Hut, where the climb begins, and still about 1,560 feet below the summit.

“It could be said I underestimated the Matterhorn myself in 2005,” Abegg told me. “Had we continued, it’s entirely possible we could have gotten into trouble.”

This past summer, Abegg returned, climbing the Hörnli Ridge with a partner before completing a solo, unsupported round trip from Zermatt in 10 hours, 8 minutes, and 19 seconds—the fastest women’s time then recorded on the FKT website, supported or unsupported. A month later, Kalie McCrystal lowered the record to 6 hours, 47 minutes, and 33 seconds.

The route’s moderate technical grade, fixed ropes, and popularity can make the Hörnli Ridge seem approachable. But finding the line and staying on solid rock demands attention. Stray from the standard route and the rock can become looser. Altitude, changing weather, and fall consequences add to the difficulty.

During Abegg’s partnered ascent this past summer, a washing-machine-sized boulder was accidentally dislodged. It tumbled down a gully, triggering what she described as a significant rockslide, mostly off route. Higher up, loose rock littered the climbing line. Abegg described rocks ranging in size from marbles to baseballs, or even volleyballs, that climbers could knock onto people below. The terrain, she said, had historically remained under snow year-round.

“Had to move very carefully,” she wrote. Guides stopped taking clients up the route during her trip.

Aside from the omnipresent risk of rockfall in any alpine environment, a 2025 study found that climate change has caused an increase in rockfall on the Matterhorn as permafrost thaws. Just a couple months ago, German online magazine Lacrux published an article about the increasing hazards of rockfall on the Matterhorn, as well as on Mont Blanc.

“Having the innate mountain sense to know when to call it is a valuable quality on an objective like this,” Abegg said.

Andy Hansen, an IFMGA-certified (International Federation of Mountain Guides) guide based in Longmont, Colorado, has guided clients on the Matterhorn twice. Speaking from his own experience, he strongly recommends hiring a guide for a first attempt.

He said recreational climbers in Western Europe are generally more accustomed to hiring guides than their counterparts in the United States. One advantage of hiring a guide on the Hörnli Ridge is how closely they follow variable conditions on a route, according to Hansen.

“The local guides have an intimacy with the mountain that gives them the advantage of having the route finding dialed, understanding the conditions of the mountain from day to day, and knowing where and when to move quickly to manage the rockfall hazard,” Hansen told me.

Hansen observed an unusual amount of rockfall in the Alps this past spring and summer, calling the Hörnli Ridge noticeably more unstable. He pointed to local guides’ familiarity with the ridge and their day-to-day knowledge of its conditions. A weather forecast can tell any climber how warm it’s likely to get, but knowing the ridge helps a guide judge which sections are most prone to rockfall, where to move quickly to limit exposure, and whether to climb that day at all.

However, whether a guide would have changed the outcome for Liner is an entirely different question. “It’s virtually impossible to say with any degree of certainty that had this party been with a mountain guide, the outcome would have been any different,” Hansen said. In his view, it was the kind of misfortune that could befall a guided party, too.

Hawkins told Climbing that they were aware of the risk of rockfall and had accepted it as a possible and uncontrollable hazard that you can’t “really do anything about.” He added that he never considered hiring a guide because he has sufficient experience and wants to take on alpine objectives independently. “If you do hire a guide, you didn’t climb the mountain,” he said of his philosophy.

While a guide is not required to climb the Matterhorn, it does materially improve your chances of reaching the summit. According to Global Summit Guide, an independent, research-based mountaineering resource based in Utah, the summit rate varies considerably depending on whether climbers are traveling with a guide.

A Global Summit Guide report updated this past July states that while the overall Matterhorn success rate is 55%, guided climbers see a 72% success rate, while unguided climbers hover around a 38% success rate. Meanwhile, first-timers like Liner and Hawkins only have an 18% shot at reaching the top. Furthermore, during the popular climbing season of May through October, October has the lowest success rate of 22%.

Global Summit Guide also reinforces the Matterhorn’s reputation as Europe’s most deadly mountain, with an average of eight to 12 fatalities annually. They note that about 1 in 140 climbers perish in their attempt to summit. More than 500 people (and counting) have died on the Matterhorn to date.

Dialogue and debate over the broader trends indirectly related to Liner’s death have already  emerged in the climbing community.

After Liner died, a Reddit thread in r/Mountaineering sparked debate about the climbing-related content he and Hawkins had posted on their Instagram accounts. “Obviously, there are videos of me and him partying in Europe, but when we’re actually climbing, I take precautions and I’m not an idiot when I climb,” Hawkins told Climbing. “I take safety as a number one precaution.” He added that Liner would “probably be laughing” at what Hawkins sees as misinformed comments online.

Then, in an Instagram reel posted on November 2, Washington-based gear manufacturer High Mountain Gear turned the discussion toward a different topic: a video Norwegian climber Magnus Midtbø made about his 2025 Matterhorn solo. High Mountain Gear took particular issue with Midtbø looking up how to use crampons shortly before his climb. In the comments of High Mountain Gear’s reel, some agreed that a climber with Midtbø’s reach ought to think about the example he sets. Others asked why he was being brought into a conversation about someone else’s accident.

Hawkins explained that he and Liner had set the Matterhorn as a big goal independent of any online content. “It’s just a climb we wanted to do for a long time,” Hawkins said of the Matterhorn. “It had nothing to do with any Instagram videos.” He noted that he wasn’t very familiar with Midtbø’s Matterhorn video.

Beyond this recent incident, when Midtbø’s video came out, Swiss public broadcaster SRF reported that Midtbø talked openly about his limited preparation. He struggled with the altitude and got off route. Other climbers had to call him back to the right line. Once he got down, he admitted he had underestimated the risk and urged viewers against following his example. Air Zermatt’s rescue chief Anjan Truffer told SRF that he worried viewers might still interpret Midtbø’s climb as a success, without appreciating the gap between his climbing ability and their own.

In Midtbø’s defense, however, he could have cut the moments when he was tired, lost, or scared. But he chose to leave them in. Some viewers in the YouTube comments took the climb as a cautionary tale. Others wanted a follow-up with a guide explaining where things nearly went wrong. Ultimately, given the irrelevance of Midtbø’s video to Hawkins’s and Liner’s Matterhorn objective, as well as the full disclosures that Midtbø provided in his video, the notion that YouTube content is to blame for this or any other fatality seems besides the point.

As a guide, Hansen sees responsibility on both sides of the screen. He said creators like Midtbø have some accountability for what they put out, even when they include a disclaimer. But viewers must assess whether their own skills match the demands of any climb described in online content.

Abegg’s father came home with a story about soloing the Matterhorn in a T-shirt. Abegg and her sister came home with a story about turning around at the Solvay Hut. Midtbø came home, too. But in his video, you can see how close he came to a different outcome when he lost the route on exposed terrain.

Kieran Liner didn’t come home. He was 20 years old. The mountain doesn’t care what drew you there, whose story you heard, or how long you spent preparing. Even the most experienced climber can be in the wrong place at the wrong time, especially when it comes to escalating hazards like rockfall.

Liner’s family is planning to celebrate his life in Pensacola and Austin. In her obituary, Newman invited everyone who knew him, shared his adventures, or found inspiration in his life to join them. “Whether you knew him for a lifetime or crossed paths with him only briefly,” she wrote, “you are part of the story he leaves behind.”

Climbing Magazine reached out to Kyle Willis of High Mountain Gear and Magnus Midtbø for comment, but have not received a response.

#8226. The Best Cross-Country Skis of 2027

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

What to know: Testers in the Midwest and Maine put more than 56 demo cross-country skis to the test. They named the Salomon Escape Outpath 65 Grip Cross-Country Skis with Prolink Bindings as the most versatile for skiing in and out of tracks. For skiers who like to go fast, they named the Fischer Speedpro 50 Skate as the best budget race ski.

Cross-country skiing is surging in popularity in the U.S. That expansion is due, in part, to the broad range of ski styles that suit every fitness level.

We tested all three styles of cross-country skis, including skate, classic, and backcountry. From a pool of 56 demo models, we evaluated skis that are optimized for beginners as well as models capable of helping accomplished skiers push their limits. From the most versatile in tracks to the best pairs for racing, these six cross-country skis impressed our testers most.

Sidecut: 60-55-65 Weight: 4 lbs 12 oz (per pair) Length: 180, 195 cm

Pros and Cons + Confidence-inspiring control + Energetic glide – Lacks flotation in snow depths greater than 4 inches

With a tip that’s barely narrower than the machine-set, 68-millimeter cross-country ski tracks grooved into Nordic trails, the versatile Escape Outpath impressed testers in all situations shy of deep snow. “It feels snappy and efficient,” reports our Maine tester after logging 20 miles on groomed and ungroomed terrain. “Very energy conserving.”

This narrow-waisted ski is a true jack-of-all-trades: It climbs, descends, easily breaks trail, and reliably floats atop several inches of fresh snow (though it became overwhelmed in more than 4 inches of powder). “It doesn’t feel squirrely on the downhills like most other skis I’ve used,” reports one novice skier.

Several design factors explain this ski’s multi-faceted performance. The three-quarter-length metal edge has a softer flex, particularly in the tip—which is built around a core made of lighter, bendier recycled ABS material that facilitates flotation on ungroomed snow. Those soft tips also adapted to other terrain features (such as the curves on classic tracks) and made this ski feel unusually easy to control in tracks and out.

A wood core and ample camber in the rest of the ski achieves a winning balance of energy and stability. “I loved the edge grip I felt on icy descents,” said one tester (who used this ski with the backcountry-oriented Salomon Escape Outrack boot). Novices appreciated its low-effort responsiveness; advanced skiers praised its playful personality and long, speed-preserving glide. In deeper snow, the Fischer S-Bound 98 Crown bested its performance, but for enjoying groomed conditions and light-duty trail-breaking, the Escape Outpath 65 was our definitive winner.

Sidecut: 85-61-75 Weight: 5 lbs 8 oz (per pair) Length: 165-195 cm

Pros and Cons + Handles mixed conditions, from firm snow to powder + Easy to turn – Heavy for a midfat

On tours that include the full range of snow conditions across mountain terrain, this ski shines. It’s narrow and stiff enough for efficient glide on flats (something that pack-laden testers appreciated as they logged miles-long commutes over frozen lakes). Its stiffness smooths the ride over chunky surfaces and provides reassuring grip on firm, wind-scoured descents. And its almost-fat width (85 millimeters at the tip) provided capable flotation in snow depths up to 10 inches.

Some of its success in mixed conditions comes from the tried-and-true pairing of a wood core with full metal edges, which bite into firm snow and provide a stable platform on chunky, cut-up slopes. Yes, that layup emphasizes stability over weight savings: It’s heavier than the Fischer S-Bound 98 Crown, for example, but more reassuring when sidehilling or descending through chop. The scaled bases delivered a likeable balance of grip and glide, and for steep climbs, attaching kicker skins ($150, sold separately) delivers skimo capability.

If cruising through touring centers is all you’ll do, the BC85 might be overkill. But if you need a versatile, all-conditions ski that performs reliably on off-piste mountain routes, here’s your winner.

Sidecut: 98-69-88 Weight: 4 lbs 9 oz (per pair) Length: 159-189 cm

Pros and Cons + Light enough for longer tours + Best-in-test grip – Lacks stability on firm conditions

If fresh pow is what lures you onto the hills, here’s your joystick. This perennial favorite still earns high scores for being floaty yet light—and its bases dazzled testers with their best-in-test performance. “The scales gripped great in all conditions, even refrozen granular, and they never clumped up when I hit mixed-temperature snow that caused icing problems for other skis,” reported one tester.

Though it’s not the floatiest of them all, the S-Bound 98 Crown proved easier to turn in deep snow. Its lightweight paulownia wood and fiberglass core has hollow air channels throughout. Not only does the fiberglass reinforcement make the ski stronger than one with a solid wood core, but the air chambers distribute pressure better, too. A rockered tip preserves the ski’s underfoot camber while also floating to the surface and facilitating turns in deep, untracked snow. On our testing trip near Maine’s Medawisla Hut, narrow steel edges helped one novice skier feel confident on smooth, groomed descents, while the wide tips provided good flotation in 18 inches of freshies.

For touring on steeps, Fischer’s two compatible mohair and nylon skins—the short “EZ Skin” or the full-length “Super Skin”—create a lightweight skimo setup.

Sidecut: 41-44-44 Weight: 2 lbs 6 oz (per ski) Length: 168-204 cm

Pros and Cons + Light, stable, and affordable + Edgehold remains on uphills – Best for beginners

Learning to skate ski requires coordination, making stability especially important in a beginner ski. But a stable beginner ski is often heavy, which can lead to fatigue. That’s why our testers gravitated toward Fischer’s entry-level race ski, the Speedpro Skate 50, as their beginner pick. It’s light and stable, but still affordable—all helpful ingredients for a first-timer.

To shave grams, Fischer built the Speedpro Skate 50 with the same “air core” construction used in its elite-level skis. Think of the ski’s core as a rectangular box made of ultralight wood. Inside, thin, wave-shaped walls of basalt-reinforced resin run the length of the ski, with air pockets in between. A lightweight fiberglass laminate reinforced with basalt fibers wraps the core, adding strength and torsional stiffness without much weight.

To improve stability, Fischer widened its contact areas and used a World Cup-level base that provides easy glide in a wide variety of snow temperatures. To add a hair more speed, they shaped it with a narrow, 41 millimeter tip that gave it an edge, especially on uphills.

Two testers used the Speedpro Skate 50 in varying snow conditions—sometimes all in the same day. During one 10-kilometer ski at Duluth’s Spirit Mountain Nordic Center after a late-spring storm, they started out in slushy, mashed potato snow at the bottom then climbed a few hundred feet to where the skate track was still frozen and riddled with chunks of ice that had fallen from trees. But the skis made it possible to steadily glide through the crud without a twist of the knee or ankle.

Sidecut: 44-43-44 Weight: 2 lbs 2 oz (per pair) Length: 177-192 cm

Pros and Cons + Super stable + Binding is adjustable on the fly – Not as playful as other skis in its class

Salomon’s new Equipe Pro replaces the S/Max. The improved ski is 20 percent lighter, a feat accomplished by replacing the foam core with the brand’s in-house “Innowave” technology. Salomon’s air core, previously reserved for elite-level race skis, is engineered from paper and glue and encased by ultralight wood sidewalls—visualize a sidecut from the corrugated wall of a cardboard box, but exponentially stronger.

Even with the ski’s dramatic weight savings, it still feels grounded and stable underfoot, a hallmark of Salomon. The almost-always-in-control feeling is largely a result of the ski’s stiff flex profile (or the stiffness of the ski’s camber), which influences speed and turning. The Equipe Pro’s outer laminate is fiberglass from tip to tail, which is heavier than the thin-ply carbon used on elite-level skis, but it also provides stability while edging.

Our testers had fun using the Equipe Pro during a leisurely ski at Wisconsin’s Superior Municipal Forest, a mostly flat course interspersed with beautifully-groomed, fun, steep, and fast rollers. On their next time out, they took it up a notch on the 25-kilometer “Picnic Loop,” a series of seemingly endless and unforgiving hills deep in the Superior National Forest. Thanks to soft new snow and the comfort and stability of the Equipe Pro, they returned with limbs intact, which isn’t always the outcome on this remote and tiring loop.

Sidecut: 44-44-43 Weight: 665 g (per ski, 196cm, with the binding installed) Length: 178-205 cm

Pros and Cons + Works well in almost every condition + Comes with a durable, 100-percent mohair skin – Quick studies may quickly outgrow this beginner-to-intermediate ski

The Atomic Pro C2 Skintec has been a top seller in Atomic’s lineup for ten years. But in late 2025, Atomic gave it a substantial makeover, shaving its weight by about eight percent, improving the camber to make it easier to kick, and simplifying the lengths and flexes.

The core is lightweight polyurethane foam (Densolite 300). Above and below that foam layer are fiberglass laminates. Carbon laminates are the go-to on higher-end skis, but fiberglass offers its own rewards—skiers can flatten the ski’s camber with less effort, which makes the kick easier. Fiberglass is also less springy than carbon, so the skis feel more stable and grounded, an attribute that stood out to both of our testers.

Of the six pairs of classic skis our tester sampled, the Pro C2 Skintec was best in all kinds of crazy backward conditions, from springtime slush in February to sub-arctic single digits in March.

As a bonus, the Pro C2 Skintec includes a set of 100 percent mohair skins, which offer the best combination of durability and water resistance and is simple to replace when it wears out (generally after 1,000 kilometers of skiing.)

Olympic racers compete in two dominant forms: Skate, in which skiers use a V-shaped stride that maximizes speed, and classic, using a parallel ski stance that looks like walking but with more glide. Both ski styles are intended for groomed cross-country ski trails, and both are accessible to newbies as well as elites.

A third type of cross-country ski is dedicated to off-trail adventure. Backcountry skis are generally wider for better flotation in uncompacted snow, with fish-scale texture on their bases that provide enough grip to stride uphill and glide down. While some classic skis have scaled bases, most—and all skate skis—rely on wax to deliver the desired balance of grip and glide.

When buying cross-country skis, it’s easy to get intimidated by Nordork speak, a tech-heavy vocabulary including terms like flex pattern, torsional stiffness, camber, grind, sidecut, and adjectives like soft, medium, stiff, extra stiff, cold, warm, and universal—all of which can apply to a different version of the same ski. Even Nordic ski manufactures admit it’s a little much, and the reason the industry is making a concerted effort to simplify the jargon for the sake of confused consumers.

Before you invest in new skis, take a ski lesson. If none are available in your area, there are some good tutorials online, including REI’s “Classic Cross-Country Skiing for Beginners” and “How To Skate Ski.” A good ski coach can break down technique in a way that makes it fun and easy to learn right off the bat so you can spend your remaining ski career feeling joy rather than frustration.

And before you buy a ski, it’s ideal to test it first—either at a race, festival, or shop that offers demo skis. It’s also a good idea to pick the brain of the Nordic manager in the ski shop who can direct you to the best ski for your weight and ability level (usually categorized as beginner, endurance/intermediate, and race).

For the backcountry test, Kelly Bastone organized two large-group testing sessions in February and March in Maine. One took place on trails around Carrabasset Valley. Some testers skied to the Poplar Stream Hut, part of Maine Huts and Trails network, for a mid-afternoon warmup with the hut’s complimentary tea and cocoa by the fire. Conditions were beautifully cold snow: five inches of fresh, compacted in places, with no ice or crust. The other session took place on a tester’s family property in central Maine in conditions that presented sun-warming snow on top of cold, fresh snow—a perfect recipe for clumping, which were also good conditions for testing. Bastone then tested skis closer to home in Yarmouth in variable conditions, involving crust layers and refrozen slush. It wasn’t ideal snow, but it was telling.

Stephanie Pearson and fellow tester Brian Hayden took the long approach to testing classic and skate skis, skiing over the course of four months in every condition. On weekdays, they rotated between five trail systems in Duluth and nearby Superior, Wisconsin. On weekends, they ventured farther north and east. It turned out to be a banner snow year in the upper Midwest with some of the best, most consistent snow in the country, from cold Styrofoam snow in December and January to perfect corduroy decks in February to corn snow in March. Even in early April, Pearson and Hayden were still skiing.

Category Manager Kelly Bastone moved to the Colorado Rockies in 1998 and has pursued outdoor sports ever since. A freelancer who writes about gear and other outdoor topics for publications such as Backpacker, AFAR, and The Red Bulletin, Bastone has contributed many gear reviews to Outside over the years. An avid skier (resort, Nordic, and backcountry), fly-fisher, mountain biker, and mushroom forager, she gets the news she needs from the weather report.

Category manager Stephanie Pearson grew up in Duluth, cross-country skiing out her backyard. Realizing her skate skiing needed a tune-up, this season she took skate-skiing lessons with Kara Salmela, a former Olympic biathlete who coaches through Duluth XC Ski Club. Pearson started at Outside as an intern in 1995 and has worked on staff and as a contributing editor for three decades. She is also a National Geographic Explorer.

#8225. 7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

Andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred. They bore witness to her exceptional first 60 miles, during which she took the lead in under-course-record pace, all the way through to her gritting out the remaining 40 miles to a ninth-place finish. They spoke with Linden after the race to find out what she learned—and why she’s already angling to come back.

Despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried. I had followed her for the final half mile, camera rolling as her leg visibly seized up, likely from cramping. She had run 60 miles at course record pace, but still had forty to go—a long way without a fully functioning lower half. Linden sat on a chair and talked through the situation with her crew. A shoe switch, a lot more electrolytes, and roll the dice. Before I get into how the rest of her race played out, let me back up.

Being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no plans for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job. This is exactly what my business partner Nick and I did after getting the call to document Des Linden’s first 100-mile race at the Javelina Jundred on October 31.

After landing in Salt Lake City, we picked up a camper van from Roadsurfer, threw our bags in the back, and headed south on I-15. A quick stop in Moab for a 50K race of our own was followed by four days evading floods and trying to figure out which desert roads were impassable after the recent downpours—which turned out to be pretty good foretelling for the race itself.

On the three previous occasions we’ve attended this event, it has been a delightful closing chapter to the season; Javelina has served as a sort of reward for making it to the end of our race coverage for the year, where the burden of logistics is removed from the job of filming. Instead of chasing athletes across the dirt roads of the Sierra Nevada at the Western States 100 or around a heavily glaciated massif at UTMB, the athletes at Javelina run in circles back to you. Five circles, to be exact. Adding to the enjoyment factor, Javelina is typically a giant Halloween party with racers and spectators dressed in costume under the warm desert sun.

However, this year was a little different. Deluge after deluge in the 24 hours leading up to the race saturated the race course. The sky relented just before the gun went off, but by the time the race had ended, over two more inches of precipitation had fallen. Not exactly what you expect for an event in the arid Sonoran Desert outside Phoenix, Arizona, but that’s why we love ultrarunning.

We did our best to keep the cameras dry and our bodies warm as we followed Linden on her third ultra—well, fourth, if you count the road 50K world record. Despite a stunning road running resume, Linden was quick to point out that she’s still a newbie at trails and ultras but is excited to keep learning. Javelina’s first three laps were nearly perfect. But soon after her body shut down it was a struggle to make it to the finish line. At one point she had to stop for almost an hour, sitting and stretching until her legs finally relaxed and let her move again. And move again she did: Linden finished her first 100-miler as the ninth woman in 16:58:01, about three hours off winner Heather Jackson. We sat down with her the day after the race to learn her biggest lessons from the process.

Linden’s biggest takeaway from Javelina is to treat 100-milers, no matter the course, weather, or circumstances, with a ton of humility. Because they ask so much of your mind and body and are a completely unique style of racing, you can’t race a 100-miler like any other distance. “Just like when I started marathons,” Linden said, “I learned that if you’re cavalier with how you race it, you’ll pay the price at some point.”

Linden was patient on her first 20-mile lap, sitting a few minutes back from the leaders. Feeling good, she picked up the pace on the next two laps, picking off all of the ladies in front of her to take the lead around the halfway mark. By the time she made it to the end of the third loop at mile 60, she had a six-minute gap on second—but her legs were starting to cramp.

Survival quickly became the goal of lap four and the best way to do that was by listening to her pacer, Magda Boulet. Thankfully, there is no one on planet Earth better suited for the job. Boulet, a fellow U.S. Olympian in the marathon, is also a Western States winner and president of GU Energy Labs. She helped coax Linden forward, made sure she kept fueling, and stuck with her through all the ups and downs.

One of Linden’s biggest challenges in the transition from road to trails and marathons to ultras is how much she needs to consume during a race—and how hard it is to catch up if she falls behind. At Javelina, Linden took most of her calories and carbs with fluids, drinking three half-liter (500 mL) bottles each lap. This fueling plan was developed for the typical heat of Javelina, but still worked well, as daytime temps almost hit 80 degrees Fahrenheit with 100% humidity.

Unfortunately, it wasn’t enough to keep her lower body from cramping around mile 60, which forced her to stop and stretch many times on the fourth lap. That setback resulted in her giving up the lead and ultimately the chance to win the race. “The fueling game has changed the sport,” Linden said. “You see it on the roads, but especially here. It’s something I will keep working on, probably forever.”

Assuming Javelina would be hot and dry like just about every other year, Linden packed for those conditions, putting her focus on cooling strategies and nutrition for the heat. She expected hardpack trails and excruciatingly hot sun, but the weather gods had other plans. Heavy rain required Linden and her crew to scramble to find key pieces of gear, including a raincoat. And because lap four took much longer than expected, Linden ran the last couple miles of it after the sun set, sans headlamp.

Next time she’ll prepare for worst-case scenarios, but will also understand when to pull the plug. “You need to know when to be tough and when it’s enough,” Linden said. “If I had to do another lap, I would have been on the edge of hypothermia and the trails were so, so slippery. There is nothing wrong with saving it for another day, but also great value in staying tough.”

Pacing strategy is different at every ultra, but there are some broad themes that apply to the majority of runners and racers, especially for someone with Linden’s ability to close in the back half if she’s feeling good. Surprisingly, this is similar to how she used to strategize for marathons. The first third should feel easy, the middle third is about keeping the pace steady, and the final third is when the racing begins. “The first three or even three-and-a-half laps are transportation,”  Linden said, “the final lap or two is about racing.”

When things got hard for Linden on the final two laps, she leaned into her crew to get to the finish. After a lap with Boulet, Linden picked up her husband Ryan as a pacer. He’s one of the most positive and energetic people you’ll ever meet, and his positivity and drive—paired with a little patience—helped get her through heavy rain and strong winds in the last 20 miles.

Her main support at Javelina HQ was Charlie Lawrence, the 100K world record holder and good friend. “A crew that knows you well, knows the sport well, and knows the emotional ups and downs of 100 miles is a real difference maker,” Linden said. “I was excited to be around everyone all week, so it was good energy going into the race, which is key.”

While Linden isn’t sure what the future holds or what her race calendar will look like next year, she walked away from the race with a surprising feeling. “I 100% want to come back to Javelina, it feels like unfinished business,” Linden said. “I didn’t think it would be this clear, but I know I can do so much better here.”

#8224. The Best Hiking Boots for Winter (2027)

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

November 2026: Our favorite winter hiking boot overall is the Salewa Puez Winter Mid Powertex for its ideal balance of warmth, comfort, and agility. It performed exceptionally well on everything from simple, cold-weather day hikes to deep snow slogs. This year, we added three new boots to the list The North Face Fastpack Mid Waterproof (Best Uninsulated), Oboz Katabatic Storm GTX (Best for Moving Fast), and the Meindl Comfort Fit Pro Hunter 300 (Best for Hunters).

While there are dozens of great three-season hiking boots on the market, winter footwear is much trickier to pull off successfully. Designers need to strike a delicate balance between the comfort, support, and agility you’d find on a fair-season hiker, and the warmth and traction you expect from your favorite pair of Sorels. Luckily, the bar gets raised every year: this season’s crop of the best winter hiking boots will go the distance, whether you’re slogging through cold muck or climbing up icy, snow-covered mountains.

Pros and Cons + No break-in required + Good in deep snow + Great grip + Light and fast – Cold below 10 degrees

Many winter boots will do the job of keeping you warm, dry, and supported—but you’ll want those straightjackets off as soon as possible. That was definitely not the case with the Puez Winters. I wore these boots on a multi-mile, deep-snow hike and a couple of muddy slogs, and then kept them on during the road trip home. I even wore them to work for a week straight and never once felt the need to fling them off.

All that comfort comes from smart shoe design—a well-engineered heel cup that kept my blister-prone foot snugly in place without feeling like a vice grip, a lightweight build (each boot comes in at one pound for a men’s size 10), a cushy hemp midsole, and a just-right rigidity that made them great for scrambling, but not ski-boot stiff.

These were not the warmest boots we tested, but they were up to the challenge down to 6 degrees Fahrenheit, as long as we were moving. That heat retention comes from a felt lining around the collar, 200 grams of Primaloft Gold insulation in the toe box, a 2.5mm wool and cotton lining around the upper, and a felt-lined footbed. Anchorage, Alaska-based tester Charlie Ebbers wore them non-stop for several days after a late fall snowstorm and said his toes were warm and happy while walking the dog, working on his cabin, grocery shopping, and even during some night hiking.

The boots shed slush and snowmelt thanks to a PFAS-free waterproof Powertex membrane, even keeping my feet dry while standing in an icy river for 40 minutes straight. All our testers found the grippy outsole ideal for staying upright on packed snow or steep, rocky trails thanks to aggressive toe and heel lugs.

Hunters who plan to sit around in the snow for hours on end scoping out animals should look elsewhere (try the more heavily insulated Mendl boot below), but for everyone else who wants to get out and explore the world from November through March, the Puez is a well-balanced choice.

Pros and Cons + Wide toe box + Just-right sole stiffness + Warm – No women’s sizes – Bulky

The Comfort Fit Pro Hunter 300 beat out our previous pick for hunters, Meindl’s Air Revolution Alpine Pro 200. That’s thanks to the Comfort Fit’s sole, which is twice as flexible as the Alpine Pro, providing better ground-feel, and its upper, which feels more like a regular hiking boot and less like something you’d use to climb an 8,000-meter peak. This boot is no slouch, though, with a full-grain nubuck upper and a rubber rand that protects from thrashing on rocks or bushwhacking off trail. A Gore-Tex membrane makes them as waterproof as any boot on the market; we found it blocked snowmelt and pouring rain admirably.

Another big plus is the wide toe box. I wore the boots on several deer-hunting hikes in the San Juan Mountains as well as around town and found the toe box nearly as comfy as what you would find in running shoes made by natural-feel brands Altra or Topo. And, although the lacing is imposing-looking, Meindl’s proprietary pattern let me get a snug fit that cut down on heel movement and eliminated ankle rub.

As the name implies, 300 grams of synthetic Gore Air Fibre insulation deliver warmth on the coldest days. I stood around in snowbanks for 45 minutes and my feet never felt cold. When actively bushwhacking on a deer or elk hunt, the boots will easily keep your feet warm, even in temperatures below zero. The Vibram Multigrip 6.0 outsole was plenty grippy and held to everything from slippery rocks to slippery branches. It also kept me on my feet while descending steep terrain.

My only niggle? The Pro Hunter 300s look a little like moon boots. They’re not particularly heavy for big, high-cut, insulated winter boots at just 2.6 pounds (per-boot), but they are bulky, making them less than ideal for scrambling.

Pros and Cons + Relatively breathable + No break-in period + Good-looking – Low Cuff

In recent years, Salomon has earned a reputation in the fashion industry, with celebs like Bradley Cooper and Snoop Dogg sporting flashy hikers from the brand. The Snowpilots have plenty of swagger, with chunky lugs, a sleek build, and a two-tone color scheme. They’re also stellar boots for cold-weather hiking, making them some of the best city-to-trail crossover duds for winter.

The Snowpilots got top marks during a winter Editor’s Choice testing trip in Maine’s 100 Mile Wilderness. These boots kept our editors’ feet toasty, even during a winter snowstorm that brought biting, blowing winds and temps in the low teens. That’s thanks to Salomon’s 70-percent-recycled polyester insulation and a soft fleece cuff. While snowshoeing up the North Summit of Shaw Mountain in two-foot-deep powder, the boot’s waterproof membrane and PU-coated leather upper blocked moisture out completely, while a breathable liner wicked sweat away during steep climbs.

The downside to these boots? A four-inch cuff height that failed to keep deeper snow from sneaking in, making them better-suited to packed trails. After the snowshoeing expedition, testers walked dogs in snowy neighborhoods around Yarmouth, Maine and went on shorter jaunts to test traction on icy trails and in slick parking lots. Deep, widely-spaced treads dug into fresh snow well, they reported, but the traction wasn’t exceptional on ice.

The Snowpilots’ fit is generous for Salomon’s typically narrow sizing, with a wider toe box, which was welcome for testers wearing thicker winter socks. Thankfully, the midfoot and heel cup were still plenty snug for testers, minimizing slippage.

Pros and Cons + Breathable + Great rebound + Sticky on wet ground – Cold when not moving

In a warming world, non-insulated winter boots are more relevant than ever. The North Face Fastpack is my top choice for the category. It works in wet, muddy, or snowy conditions—thanks to the waterproof, high-cut upper—but is also a great temperate, dry-weather hiker with a bouncy sole that helped me put in long miles on rocky and brush-covered trails.

The midsole is made from TNF’s nitrogen-infused EVA “Dream” foam, which I found to be cushy but stable on rocky terrain in the Sandia Mountains outside Albuquerque, and on packed snow up in the San Juan Mountains of southern Colorado. A ripstop nylon upper with TPU reinforcements put up with rocks, branches, and crusty snow, and the brand’s proprietary waterproof membrane didn’t let any moisture in and was breathable in temps up to the 50s. Five-millimeter lugs on the proprietary outsole rubber gripped everything from kitty litter rocks to melting ice.

I wore the Fackpacks in temps down to the low 30s, and as long as I was wearing a thick merino sock, my feet were fine. These boots, however, are meant for hikers who are always on the move—they let cold in quickly when you’re spending idle time in the snow. They are ideal for places with a tame winter (like New Mexico), and pull double-duty on wet, shoulder-season excursions anywhere.

Pros and Cons + Slim and sleek + Not too warm + Stable on rough terrain – Poor ankle support – Hard to pull on

Winter is not the time when most Fastest Known Times (FKTs) are set. But that doesn’t stop hikers from moving fast in the off-season. Oboz’s Katabatic Storm GTX is designed to enable that small niche of hikers.

Unlike other insulated boots that bulk up from all the insulation, the Katabatic Storm GTX feels as sleek as a regular hiking boot. To keep the boots nimble but still protect from the elements, Oboz used a slim layer of proprietary breathable foam insulation over the tongue, toe, and underfoot, and lined the entire boot with a Gore-Tex membrane. I noticed the chill seeping in from the non-insulated spots, but as long as I was moving, my feet were never cold, even trudging through fresh snow in temps as low as 15 degrees in Lake Tahoe, California.

This was the only winter boot I tested that came with grab-and-pull cinchable speed lacing system. It made for a snug, precise fit, and the zippered covers kept debris out. On the downside, I had a hard time pulling the boots on through the narrow, elastic foot entry between the heel collar and the tongue. I also found the flexible ankle insufficient for carrying a heavy pack.

That said, the Katabatic Storm GTX is sturdy and protective. A compression-molded EVA midsole struck a nice balance between stable and responsive, providing more rebound than what you normally find on a winter hiker. A robust toe guard helped when I was scrambling through high-alpine chunk in Colorado during a late-winter hike, and five-millimeter lugs on the Vibram IceTrek outsole stuck to snow and rock with total confidence.

When you’re adventuring in the wettest and coldest conditions, keeping your feet dry and warm is essential. Crafted specifically for cold weather outdoor activities, these faux shearling-lined boots are 100% waterproof to protect against anything and everything. The molded BioLite footbed and non-marking slip-resistant outsole maximize grip and comfort while the rear and front pull tabs make it easy to slip them on and off. They come in men’s and women’s models plus a variety of colors.

Pros and Cons + Grippy on ice + Comfy out of the box + Versatile medium-high collar – Not meant for extreme cold – Ugly

The Expeditionist Extreme Winter Boot, despite its formidable name, is the ideal everyday boot: Not exceptional at any one thing, but pretty good at everything and very comfortable. They’re a one-size-fits-all solution if you like spending time outside when it’s cold, but don’t want to go too far or stay out too long.

This boot is ideal for casual snowshoers. The high cuff keeps out snow, while a flexible-but-sturdy midsole feels offers just the right amount of bend and lateral support for a binding. The boot has a nice, bouncy step with good energy return, and felt ideal on hikes in the three- to five-mile range—although it felt underpowered on bigger days. Columbia’s proprietary outsole material, Omni-Grip Ice, and wide-spaced lugs did a better job than most of keeping our testers planted during a mid-winter trip in northern Maine.

Moderate cold wasn’t an issue for our testers thanks to the boot’s 400 grams of synthetic insulation. When temps got really low, however, thick woolen socks were a necessity: Ice fisherman and road workers who have to stand around in the cold all day should look elsewhere. But for mixed, slushy conditions, testers appreciated Columbia’s proprietary waterproof/breathable membrane, which never leaked a drop and allowed for some ventilation in a wide range of temps (teens to mid-40s).

Our testers’ biggest complaint? These boots aren’t exactly easy on the eyes with a somewhat top-heavy, bloated upper and muted colorways. But if you’re looking for a purely utilitarian winter boot for moderate conditions, these boots will provide versatile comfort day in and day out.

Pros and Cons + Cushy midsole + Very warm + Impressive grip – Expensive – Too bulky for some traction devices

Hoka is well known for helping kick off the chunky midsole trend in hiking boots and trail runners. With the Kaha 2 Frost GTX, you get all the cush of your favorite warm-weather boot, along with the giant heel brake, but pumped up with gobs of insulation to keep your feet warm on the coldest days.

Thanks to all the cushioning, these boots were great for long, demanding miles. I clambered over chunky scree, across manky snow, and through sticky mud on several nine- and 10-mile mixed-terrain hikes in the Sandia Mountains outside Albuquerque, New Mexico. Even though my quads were worked from the distance, my feet were totally unscathed thanks to a squishy, dual-density, compression-molded EVA midsole and the signature forked, extended heel, which saved energy and helped with downhill braking. The only downside to that jumbo heel? It makes compatibility with traction devices, like microspikes, iffy. We had to go up a full size just to fit them over the front and back lips of the Frost GTX.

Unlike most active winter boots, which use a lighter 200 grams of insulation, Hoka stuffs its Kaha Frost with 400 grams—a mix of synthetic insulations from Gore and Primaloft—plus a layer of aluminum lining in the sole. The tongue, too, has 400 grams of Primaloft Gold. I wore these boots on a five-degree day gathering firewood outside El Valle, New Mexico, and my feet were plenty warm. In temps above freezing, you’ll quickly overheat in these Gore-Tex-wrapped ovens.

At nearly $300, the Hokas are an investment. But if you live in a perpetually-cold part of the world, these boots are your ticket to pain-free miles in the snow.

Pros and Cons + High collar keeps snow out + Surprisingly lightweight + Durable – Pricey – Some break-in needed

Slipping on a pair of Ursas feels like suiting up for a medieval duel. With a 10-inch collar, stiff sole, and a substantial rubber rand around the entire foot, these boots are true winter armor. The Ursas kept us protected while bushwhacking up steep terrain on hunting trips, cutting firewood in the dead of winter, and slogging through frozen construction sites.

We put in plenty of testing time on longer trails to make sure a boot this burly wasn’t going to kill our feet. Testers took it slow for the first couple hikes, and were pleasantly surprised that the boots started to break in after just a few days. No one got blisters or complained of major foot fatigue. (The boots’ 3.8-pound weigh-in, however, didn’t exactly inspire us to tackle 30-mile days.)

Despite the high cuff, the Ursas were easy to slip on and never felt like they held us back from moving fluidly, even on a 15-mile day in mixed conditions that included plenty of snow and mud. We found that the suede and nylon cuff (which took a full minute to lace up properly), provided extra confidence and padding that a gaiter simply couldn’t, comfortably protecting us as we tore through brush and snow off-trail and used the boots to brace felled trees while operating a chainsaw. The ultra-aggressive Vibram outsole was overkill for walks down dirt paths, but proved ideal in mud and snow where muck-evacuating lugs kept us stable.

We put the Ursas into rotation instead of the Meindl Air Revolution Alpine Pro 200 any time we were heading out into exceptionally deep snow or mud. We found the Ursa’s construction,  with a full-length shank, to be just as supportive as the Meindl’s when it came to hauling heavy loads, whether it was tree rounds or meat.

Lacrosse offers this boot in both insulated and non-insulated versions. The non-insulated pair allows an extended seasonal range: wearing them on warmer days into the 60s, we found that our feet got a little sweaty when working hard, but not so sweaty that we felt like pulling the boots off. And with wool socks, they felt cozy down to around 20 degrees. With the insulated version, which adds 400 grams of Primaloft Gold synthetic, you can expect to keep those toes toasty down to 0-degrees, but they’re swampy above 40.

The first question to ask about buying winter hikers: Where and how will I use them? Do you live in Colorado and love to snowshoe, or are you down in Georgia and just in need of something waterproof and warmer than a three-season boot? Will you be running and fast-packing in the boots, or carrying an elk over rough terrain and sitting around a campfire? Narrowing down your use-case is absolutely necessary because winter hikers are more specific in their design than normal hikers—you don’t want to get stuck with a boot that’s too warm, heavy, or stiff, or one that lacks adequate insulation and support. To help you make the right choice, here are the factors you’ll want to consider.

In our testing, most synthetic insulations are similar in terms of warmth. Pay less attention to the type of insulation and more to the amount. Hikers that will keep you warm in the snow but not overheat your foot often come with about 200 grams of insulation. Some boots also use reflective liners or threads, similar to space blanket material, to bounce heat back at the wearer. Others use air or gas-filled aerogels, particularly around the toe area. Unless you’re heading for very cold climates or doing a lot of standing around, be aware that boots with heavy and varied insulation can cause sweaty, blistered feet.

Just like winter tires that are designed to perform on snow and ice, some winter hikers come with outsoles made of soft rubber compounds that remain flexible in cold temperatures. Vibram’s Artic Grip outsole, for example, has a proprietary compound that makes a noticeable difference in terms of traction on wet ice. Lug design is a factor, too: tiny, biting teeth for gripping snow and large voids for evacuating slush can make all the difference. Be aware that no outsole can provide sure-footedness on ice, no matter the compound used, and traction aids, like microspikes or crampons, are often necessary.

If you’re serious about winter hiking, your boot should have a waterproof membrane. We’ve seen folks head out with treated leather boots, and they never perform as well as a tried-and-true Gore-Tex (or similar) membrane. We’re sticklers about moisture, because wet, cold feet can mean the end of your hike—or worse.

Like all boots, winter hikers will tear your feet to pieces if they don’t fit well. Even if you can’t try on your preferred boots at a local store, go ahead and order them, wear them around your house for a couple days, and make sure your foot isn’t screaming to get out. You’ll want to pay attention to things like heel slippage (which causes blisters), toe space (too little can cause bruising on the downhill), overall width, ankle support, and how easy they are to pull on and off.

How much insulation you need depends where you live and hike. If you live in a moderate area where temps seldom drop below freezing, you can get away with a regular hiking boot and a thick merino sock. If you spend a lot of time in frigid temps and snow, an insulated boot will make you significantly more comfortable. Winter-specific insulated boots also tend to come with outsoles designed for better grip on snow and ice.

Like any piece of specialized outdoor equipment, you’re paying for all the incorporated technology. The extra cost comes from the insulation, the specialized outsoles, and the waterproof liners that ensure your feet stay dry.

We suggest the Salomon X Ultra Snowpilot Waterproof. It has an approachable pricepoint, isn’t heavy or bulky, and provides a lot of warmth in frigid temps.

If you buy a boot with a waterproof membrane, that membrane will keep your feet dry even if you spend hours in the snow. Your foot could still get wet if snow sneaks into the top of the boot or you work up a sweat—even the best waterproof-breathable linings are limited in efficacy.

To put these boots through their paces, we set out to the coldest, snowiest places we could find, from Alaska to Bavaria, Germany. Testers ran the gamut from carefree van dwellers who were criss-crossing the country to winter athletes to moms and dads with just a few hours to burn off steam. During the test we clomped through fresh snow, tried our best to slip in icy parking lots, strapped into snowshoes, post-holed on late-winter hikes, and stood around in snowbanks to see how long it took for our feet to go numb. But most importantly, we put in miles. If a boot wasn’t comfortable, supportive, and reliable, it didn’t make our list.

Category manager Jakob Schiller is a gear columnist for Outside. Over a decade of footwear testing, he guesses that he’s worn over 250 pairs of hiking boots. Winter is his favorite season by far, so he’s happiest when spending time on the snow and in the woods.

Charlie Ebbers is a long-time Outside contributor and an avid runner and hunter who lives in Alaska and works for the BLM. For the past year he’s been building a cabin in rural Alaska and frequently tests shoes in temps that are well below zero.

Kip Malone has tested footwear for Outside for the past seven years and is known as the team’s resident crank because of his hard-to-please feet. As a Seattle, Washington native, he is the authority on waterproof boots.

Kay Matthews is Jakob Schiller’s mom and she has hiked all across New Mexico and Colorado for the past five decades. She’s published hiking guides to the Sandia and Sangre de Cristo mountains, taught hiking classes through the University of New Mexico’s continuing education department, and still covers a lot of miles even though she’s 76.

#8223. Iran Executed a Mountaineer for Alleged Violence in Anti-Government Protests. Hundreds More Face the Same Fate.

Ali Sina Mostafavi (Photo: Courtesy of Iran Human Rights)

Ali Sina Mostafavi dreamed of climbing Everest. In 2019, he trekked to its Base Camp. Under a photo of him pointing to the summit, he wrote on Instagram in English: “Top of the world. I promise to come back to you.”

Mostafavi never fulfilled his promise. On October 14, he was executed by the Iranian authorities in Kerman Central Prison.

The 38-year-old is one of at least 39 people to have been executed in connection with Iran’s anti-government protests last winter, and one of six athletes among them.

Dr. Zohreh Abdollahkhani, an ice climber and co-founder of the Norway-based Human Rights for Sport, told Climbing, “From a human rights perspective, every single aspect of this case is an absolute violation. The state has not made any credible, independently verifiable evidence public.”

Born in 1987 in Bam County, southeastern Iran, Mostafavi was a professional mountaineer and a member of the Speeco mountaineering club in his home city of Kerman. He called mountains ‘the love of his life,’ according to Abdollahkhani.

Mostafavi climbed two of Iran’s highest peaks, Damavand (5,610m/18,410ft) and Alam-Kuh (4,850m/15,910ft). In 2016, he ascended Mount Kazbek (5,054m/16,581ft) in Georgia.

In 2019, Mostafavi traveled to Nepal and summited Island Peak (6,189m/20,305ft) and trekked to Everest Base Camp. In 2022, he attempted Ama Dablam (6,812m/22,349ft), reaching 6,600m/21,654ft.

Mostafavi was married and had a 13-year-old daughter, Respina. Alongside his climbing career, he was an accomplished musician who played the tar, a traditional Persian lute. Friends spoke of his sensitive, artistic spirit, and his deep love for mountains, music, and animals—notably, his beloved cat and dog.

On his Instagram account, @everest_coldhell, his bio reads: ‘Mount Explorer. Love the nature. Musician.’

In December 2025, Iran’s economic crisis sparked street protests that developed into nationwide demonstrations against the Islamic Republic’s repressive regime, which enforces compulsory hijab laws restricting women’s autonomy, conducts violent crackdowns on protests, issues arbitrary arrests, and employs the use of torture.

In an attempt to suppress dissent, authorities used lethal force, killing thousands and arresting tens of thousands of protesters. The human rights organization Amnesty International called this “the deadliest period of repression by the Iranian authorities” in its decades of monitoring the country.

Following the assassination of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei by US-Israeli airstrikes on February 28, Iran’s government intensified repressive crackdowns on dissent under the pretext of “wartime conditions.”

By October, at least 106 people arrested during the January protests had received death sentences, according to documentation by human rights organization Hengaw.

Iran carries out the world’s second-highest number of executions after China. In 2025, its government executed at least 2,159 people, the highest figure recorded by Amnesty International since 1981.

On Instagram, Mostafavi expressed support for Iran’s former Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, an exiled dissident who calls for a secular, democratic, and liberal Iran, describing him as “the only saviour of the homeland.” Two sources claim that Mostafavi’s family were set to move abroad before the 2022 ‘Woman, Life, Freedom’ protests began, but he ultimately chose to remain to fight for Iran’s future.

One obituary claims that he had been arrested twice in recent years for political activism and had spent time in Kerman Prison. This January, the mountaineer joined protests alongside millions of Iranians.

IranWire, an independent pro-democracy outlet, reported that Mostafavi was arrested three months later on April 25 alongside his wife, his sister, and his sister’s fiancé, while his mother’s home was also raided.

Mostafavi was reportedly beaten during his arrest and was forced to sign confession papers to release his family members. It is not known whether he had access to an independent lawyer, a right frequently denied to defendants in political and national security cases in Iran.

The Iranian judiciary’s account of the case was published by state-aligned media outlets including Mizan News Agency, Tasnim News Agency, the IRIB, and Tabnak. The allegations have not been independently verified.

The Judiciary of Iran claimed that Mostafavi had participated in the widespread anti-government protests in January, and that he was a member of the “Immortal Guards,” an armed wing of exiled dissident Reza Pahlavi’s group.

The judiciary also alleged that Mostafavi had shot and injured two civilians, fired at security forces, and possessed firearms, ammunition, and Molotov cocktails. It further accused him of communicating with foreign media and sharing footage of missile strike locations during the US-Iran war.

Mostafavi was convicted of the capital offense of moharebeh, or “enmity against God,” alongside several charges relating to alleged violence, weapons possession, and communication with hostile media. The evidence against him has not been made public.

The judiciary reported that the fiancé of Mostafavi’s sister received a prison sentence of 12 years and seven months for alleged cooperation, while he, his wife, and his sister were also sentenced to seven months in prison for posting content deemed as propaganda against the regime.

An appeal against Mostafavi’s death sentence was rejected. IranWire reported that he was transferred to solitary confinement the night before his execution and that family members were summoned. The judiciary announced that he was hanged at dawn in Kerman Central Prison on October 14. According to IranWire, Mostafavi asked the prison guards to pass along a message to the judge: “I did not wage war against God, nor did I commit moharebeh that you should charge me with it; my fight was with you.”

That evening, state-aligned outlet Tabnak published footage purporting to show Mostafavi’s arrest, weapons allegedly found in his possession, and a confession to a planned attack on Kerman Airport. IranWire reported that the confession appeared to have been made under duress and spliced together with unverified footage. Amnesty International has also identified signs of forced confessions in 18 videos of Iranian prisoners arrested between February and May 2026, during the same period as Mostafavi’s arrest.

Shortly after his death, a video of Mostafavi’s young daughter crying on her father’s grave, accompanied by their cat, circulated on social media.

Human rights groups have voiced concerns about Mostafavi’s case in the context of widespread forced confessions and sham trials lacking due process in Iran.

“The complete absence of forensic evidence or transparent court records confirms that his conviction rested entirely on forced confessions extracted under coercion rather than any objective proof,” Abdollahkhani said.

She explained that the arrest of Mostafavi’s wife, his sister, and his sister’s fiancé fits an established pattern of authorities using family members as leverage.

“The Islamic Republic routinely arrests close relatives and uses threats of torture or sexual violence to force athletes into making false confessions in a desperate bid to save their loved ones,” she said.

According to Human Rights for Sport, at least eight other mountaineers’ lives are at risk.

Maryam Hadavand Siri, a 42-year-old mother of two, led the Mountaineering Board of Pakdasht County in Tehran Province. She was arrested during the January protests, transferred to Evin Prison, and sentenced to death in April, without access to an independent lawyer. Following an appeal, her case was referred to the Supreme Court for review.

Social media activist and mountaineer Fatemeh Jami was arrested at her home on June 30 by Cyber Police officers. She was transferred to Gorgan Prison, where she remains detained without access to a lawyer or medical assistance.

Tara (Shirin) Masoudi, a member of the Razhan Mountaineering Group in Mahabad, was arrested on August 19. She was transferred to a detention centre and later released on bail. She is awaiting a final verdict.

Mohammad Hakimpour, Mostafa Ghaderi, Mohammad Saleh Hosseini, Hossein Abdollahi, and Khaled Rahimi—all members of climbing clubs in Saqqez—were arrested on October 8. According to Human Rights for Sport, they were subjected to physical abuse in detention and have been denied access to legal counsel, family visits, and telephone calls.

Abdollahkhani urges climbers to raise awareness of Mostafavi’s execution and the status of the eight other mountaineers, and to contact national federations, sports governing bodies, the International Climbing and Mountaineering Federation (UIAA), and the International Olympic Committee (IOC).

“How is it possible that a member of the climbing community is at risk of execution on alleged political charges, while the global climbing world stays silent?” she asked.

On October 30, Human Rights for Sport published an open letter to the UIAA executive board and athlete commission. In the letter, Abdollahkhani asks the UIAA to appeal directly to Iran’s national mountaineering federation, along with its Ministry of Sport and National Olympic Committee, to stop further executions and advocate for the release of imprisoned climbers.

#8222. The Historic SS United States Was Sunk off Florida to Become the World’s Largest Artificial Reef

SS United States (Photo: Destin-Fort Walton Beach)

As it turns out, it takes a lot to sink a 990-foot ocean liner.

The SS United States was supposed to start going down at 1 p.m. Central Time on Wednesday, November 11. Last-minute preparations pushed that to nearly 5 p.m. By 4:45, every valve was open, and the Gulf was pouring in. Then came four more hours of watching a ship refuse to leave. She finally slipped under at 8:59 P.M., twenty-two nautical miles southwest of Destin, Florida, in the Gulf of Mexico, tilting hard to her port side.

From a nearby boat, I watched the fastest ocean liner ever built make the slowest exit imaginable. On her maiden voyage in 1952, she beat the Queen Mary’s record by about ten hours. On Veterans Day, the iconic ocean liner needed about four hours just to go under.

With this scuttling—a deliberate, controlled sinking—the SS United States becomes the world’s largest artificial reef, surpassing the USS Oriskany, which had held the title since its 2006 sinking. It’s a second life that’s part habitat project and part tourism bet, and it follows years of failed rescue plans and a last-minute court fight.

Here’s how a ship once meant to become a museum ended up on the Gulf floor, what it means for the sea around her, and what divers can expect when they finally get to explore her underwater.

Why sink her off the Florida Panhandle? Habitat and tourism. The seafloor off Destin and Fort Walton Beach is mostly sand and shell, and natural reef is scarce. Okaloosa County’s tourism department laid out a five-year, $12 million plan to make Destin-Fort Walton Beach the dive capital of Florida, with part of the money coming from tourist-development tax revenue. Visit Pensacola and the Coastal Conservation Association’s Florida chapter signed on as partners. Part of that money funds a multiyear marketing campaign to promote the ship as a diving destination.

The SS United States is also slated to join the Florida Panhandle Shipwreck Trail. The state created the trail in 2012 to stimulate tourism, after the Deepwater Horizon oil spill. It began with twelve wrecks off Pensacola, Destin, Panama City, and Port St. Joe and has since grown to more than 20. Divers collect passport stickers at each one. These 20 ships are among 48 large vessels sunk by the county since the 1970s.

The SS United States now rests in about 180 feet of water. If she landed upright, as early sonar scanning indicates, her upper decks are roughly 50 to 60 feet down. The county says divers of all skill levels can reach the upper decks.

While there were once dreams of converting the 990-foot icon into a hotel or museum, she deteriorated to the point that the options came down to the scrapyard or an artificial reef.

The liner was abruptly withdrawn from service in 1969. She later spent nearly thirty years docked in Philadelphia, where no one managed to repurpose her.

For decades, owners kept hunting for the ship’s second act. In 2016, Crystal Cruises studied a return to sea and called the obstacles insurmountable. By the time a rent fight got the historic ship ordered off a Philadelphia pier in 2024, the nonprofit that owned the vessel says it was left with two options: scrap or “reef her”. Preservationists argue a museum ship was still possible.

The conservancy ultimately sold the liner to Okaloosa County, Florida, for $1 million. The county has spent a total of more than $13 million getting it ready to scuttle—remediation, towing, insurance, deployment—and contributing toward the yet-to-be-constructed museum dedicated to the ocean liner. The county’s tourism director calls the project an economic development opportunity and an environmental asset. Its tourism director told NPR the county expects to make back its investment in a couple of years.

A last-minute lawsuit nearly stopped the sinking. The SS United States Preservation Foundation sued the Army Corps of Engineers in federal court in Pensacola on November  3, arguing the agency failed to adequately weigh the ship’s toxic coatings under federal environmental law. Three days later, a judge denied the emergency request to halt the sinking, citing the lack of an affidavit and the cost of an injunction. An earlier suit from a separate New York group had already been dismissed in 2025.

On the whole, scuttling (or initially sinking) a properly cleaned vessel can house a new ecosystem for fish and other oceanic life. Crews drained and cleaned the fuel tanks of the SS United States, and no explosives were used. The county says it removed 99 percent of the PCB-containing materials, though nobody outside the project has independently verified that number.

The open question is the old zinc-chromate primer, which contains hexavalent chromium. Those who still wanted the ship preserved topside say it will leach. The county says it converts underwater into a less toxic form. A Drexel oceanographer called the risk “a little overblown,” while saying he’d still prefer mitigation. The Oriskany, another purpose-sunk vessel off the coast of Destin, which held the title of world’s largest artificial reef until Wednesday is a cautionary precedent. It became a thriving reef, but monitoring also found elevated PCBs in some of its fish.

Algae, barnacles, and sponges settle on the steel first. Corals can follow, then small fish, then the predators that hunt them. Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution is tracking the process at about 132 tagged spots on the wreck, with a goal of acquiring ten years of data.

Scientists still argue about whether reefs create new fish or just concentrate existing ones for anglers. Gulf red snapper research leans toward creation, though it comes mostly from oil platforms and smaller reefs, not one giant ship.

One more caveat: this is new habitat, not restoration. It was sunk in an area that was mostly sand, so no existing reef habitat was disturbed or restored. This is a net-new ecosystem for the region.

The iconic ship’s two sixty-five-foot funnels, propeller, and radar mast are headed to a land-based museum near Destin. Everything else now belongs to the Gulf.

Like the other divers who attended the sinking, I was hoping to dive it within the first 24 hours. But the rough conditions forecast for today, which pushed the sinking up one day, also kept us out of the water. I’ll be back as soon as I can to skim above the deck, but the bragging rights for the vessel’s first recreational dive are still up for grabs.

The exact date divers will have access to the new dive site is still unknown. Safety divers must clear the site before recreational divers are allowed.

Local charter operators are hoping to head out as soon as Friday. Niuhi Dive Charters says divers from all over the world have already signed up.

The county says her top deck, anticipated to be at 55 to 60 feet, is accessible to all levels of certified divers, which makes an Open Water certification the entry ticket. If you want more than a look at the top, Advanced Open Water, with its 100-foot-limit, is the better choice, and charter operators set their own requirements. Wreck and Nitrox certifications are smart additions. The lower decks belong to technical divers with decompression and trimix training.

Plan on a full day offshore. She’s about twenty-two nautical miles southwest of Destin-Fort Walton Beach, and Destin is the closest launch point. Divers can book through Niuhi Dive Charters or ScubaTech Destin, which runs daily Gulf charters aboard the Sea Cobra.

Alexandra Gillespie is the former digital editor of Scuba Diving magazine. With nearly 200 dives under her weight belt, and has covered scuba diving and marine sustainability for Outside, National Geographic, U.S. News and World, NPR, BBC, and other major publications. She’s gone diving everywhere from California’s kelp forests to Bahamian reefs to Sudan’s Red Sea.
