#8221. Watch: Jessie Diggins Explains Why Sparkles Are Her Superpower

Trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene caught up with cross-country skiing superstar Jessie Diggins in Kona, Hawaii, a few days before the Ironman World Championship. In this exclusive interview, Diggins shares how she battled through a deep low to finish (and win) her first 100-miler, the lessons from cross-country skiing that she’s applying to trail running, and why she always puts on face glitter before a race.

After retiring from cross-country skiing as the most decorated American of all time, glide off into the sunset Jessie Diggins did not. The Olympic gold medalist earned one last piece of hardware in Milan-Cortina this spring—on bruised ribs no less—hung up the skis, and dove head-first into trail running.

Diggins, 35, raced the Broken Arrow Triple Crown in June, as has become her annual ritual. She then lined up against the world’s best trail runners at Sierre-Zinal in August, won the Superior 100-miler in September, and just last weekend won the (bear with me) Trail Animals Running Club Stone Cat Trail Festival 50-miler in Massachusetts.

On paper, it’s been an effortless transition into a sport Diggins swears she is just doing for fun. But of course there is so much more to the story once you dig in. I was lucky enough to catch up with Diggins at the epicenter of yet another endurance sport—the Ironman World Championship—in Kona, Hawaii, last month. She’d just come from a snorkeling expedition trying to find a sea turtle. (So far no luck.) Gazing out onto the turquoise waves crashing into shore, we chatted about what she’s learned and loved about trail running so far. That list includes (and is not limited to) how trail running really is a team sport, achieving personal goals is bigger than the results, fueling on a “washing machine” stomach is not easy, and the power of glitter translates from snowy trails to dry ones.

This interview has been edited for clarity. You can also watch some of it above.

Jessie: It was a really cool experience. It was so humbling, but so exciting to tackle a totally different challenge. I was filled with curiosity: What will this feel like? What’s going to happen to my body? What will happen inside my brain? How does this work?

Having a crew and pacers like that is very different from skiing. [In skiing] you are alone on the trail, and people can cheer for you, but you don’t actually have anyone with you on the trail. And so it was just so exciting I got to do it with a team. That was really big for me. I’m a very team-oriented person, and I would get so excited to come into the aid station and see the crew and to get to have a pacer with me. Even when I was falling apart and couldn’t even  talk—I was at a really low point—it was just like, ‘I’m here with my team and I’m pushing my limits and I’m seeing what’s possible for me.’ And that’s so exciting.

I would just tell myself ‘every step you take is a step you don’t have to take again.’ So I was just like, ‘I’m doing it. I’m slowly working towards that finish line, step by step.’ It was so funny because even when I was deeply uncomfortable, I never actually thought about quitting, which I thought I would. It was more just like I’m so uncomfortable, but I know I can if I just keep moving. Even if I’m slowing down, even if I’m not even able to run, I have to just power hike this section. I’m still moving towards my goal. I’m in the process of getting there, and that’s exciting in and of itself.

I kind of wanted to set up a charcuterie board of the trail world and try different things because they were all so different, right? Broken Arrow is a huge festival and it was a multi-day thing, so oh my gosh, what is day three gonna feel like? Can I even run downhill on day three?

And then Sierre-Zinal is so historic, and it was such a cool course. It was beautiful, and it was like experiencing a very classic “short” trail race, right? I was like, ‘this is not short.’ It took me 3 hours, but it was so cool to experience.

And then going into the 100 miler, it was different and more of a backyard format. Or not a backyard in terms of the laps, but like there was no award ceremony. It wasn’t about winning. It was just about doing it, and I love that. That is so aligned with how I feel about racing. It’s like, ‘No, we don’t really care who wins. We just want everyone to challenge themselves and hopefully make their goal of crossing the finish line.’ And that was so cool for me.

And so getting to be a part of each of these events, I got to experience so many different angles of the trail world and meet so many people. And for me, that was a big thing, too: feeling the sense of community that was around every single race and making new friends and trying something new. That was very cool.

No, I definitely am excited to do more. I don’t know what that’s gonna look like yet, but I feel like just getting to be involved in this world is so cool and so exciting. So, I’m sort of now in the phase of like, ‘OK, I feel like I’m bouncing back with 100. Like, my body’s coming back, and now I can start dreaming and scheming and brainstorming, like what else do I want to do? What else is out there? What excites me? What feels like the appropriate challenge for this phase of my life?’ Yeah, I’m trying to figure it all out.

I think the biggest thing was in training, like listening to my body. So I stopped wearing a heart rate monitor like five or six years ago, and it was really about being in tune and listening to my body and figuring out where I can push. What does it feel like when I’m riding that line of level three, and what are the signals in my body when I’ve gone over that line and I need to pull it back?

And so really trying to deeply understand how I feel, and I feel like that’s helped me steer away from injuries too, because I’m not relying on metrics. I want to feel how my body feels and respond to that and act on those feelings.I think that’s something I’m taking with me because I’m well aware now that running can really beat you up in a different way. Even listening to my body and learning how much can I eat while I’m running because your stomach is a washing machine and that does not happen in cross-country skiing.

I think it was really exciting in my final years of cross-country skiing, learning more about high-carb fueling and having all these great products come on board. Because in a ski race, let’s say a 50-kilometer race, you come through a feed zone, but you have gloves and your hands are in poles, so you are not like ripping open a gel. You’ll end up stabbing yourself in the face. And so what you do is you tuck your poles under your armpits and you grab the feed bottle, which is usually an actual baby bottle with the lid taken off, from a coach who cannot run with you, they have to just stand there and hold it by the rim. So you grab it while you are gliding quite quickly. You down it so you get like a few good sips, and then you have to chuck the bottle on the side and keep moving. And so having really high carb drink mixes where you can, if you only can get a few mouthfuls, you need them to count, and so having these was huge. Because before it’d be like, ‘I guess we’ll boil down Coke to de-fizz it, and that’s what you can have.’ But it  just wasn’t high carb enough, and the electrolyte balance might not have been great.

Now there’s so many options, and that really changed the way I could race. And so now, in trail racing, there’s all these different gels. You can find the one that works for you. There’s all these different mixes. You can find the amount of salt that works for you. That’s been really cool. Being able to tailor it. I feel like 15 years ago, there weren’t that many options. Now having more options is power.

I do get scared. It’s funny. I just saw on the elevator this morning a woman was wearing glitter, and I was like, ‘Yes!’ That was my whole thing through my ski career. And it came out of being scared and being nervous. And I feel like people don’t always know that that’s the origin. But I would get so nervous for races, and a little bit of nerves is great. It means you care. If you’re not nervous for a race, it’s sort of like, ‘Why am I doing this?’ You know, then it’s time to maybe examine, do I really care about what I’m doing?

Like with any work project, any life thing, I think that a little bit of nerves is super healthy. It also brings out the adrenaline and it tells your body, ‘I am ready to perform.’ But I would get nervous to the point where I’m stealing all my energy, and so it was hard to take yourself too seriously when you’re actually just covered in glitter. And so I would put on the sparkles as this promise to myself, like, ‘Hey, I get to be here. I get to do this. I got to sign up for this. That’s amazing. I have an opportunity to go out there and do my best at a sport that I love with a team that I love, and that’s really cool.’ And so the glitter was my pre-race ritual of ‘I’m going to go out there and have fun and remember to smile at the start because I’m so lucky to get to do this.’ Because sport is ultimately in the entertainment category. It is literally fun and games.

At the end of the day, yes, there’s a lot of pressure. There can be expectations. There can be a lot of lights. A lot of people are watching you, but you get to do this. You get to challenge yourself and see what’s possible. And that, in and of itself, is such an amazing opportunity.

#8218. This New Book Strives to Help Climbers Rewire Their Mental Game

(Photo: Left: Sam Douglas Jones / Right: Vertebrate Publishing)

We all do it: Eyeing other climbers and comparing ourselves to them. Wishing we were better at dynos, heel hooks, or some other elusive climbing move. Loading ourselves with shoulds when it comes to training or grades.

Even non-performance-oriented climbers like me tend to be guilty of at least some negative thoughts when we’re up on the wall. It’s hard not to think that way when so many highly specific levels dominate the sport. This makes the idea of progression almost impossible to resist, even if you claim to do it only for fun.

There is something about the progress ladder of the Yosemite Decimal System. Its slash grades, letter addendums, and pluses and minuses tempt you to try and tick routes with higher grades. The same goes for the V-scale, as well as many other grading scales. We often ask “What if?” questions about breaking into a harder grade. And we often define ourselves by the grades we climb. “I’m a V10 boulderer,” someone might say, or “I’m a 5.10 climber.”

Meanwhile, when I’m skiing or mountain biking, there are essentially only four, color-coded levels, green through double black. Compared to climbing, I find it rare for someone to ask what color run I skied or trail I rode—and did I make it down without falling? But after someone climbs a route, one of the first questions might be what the grade was. And did you send it?

As the sport continues to grow, two British climbers have noticed that the expansion of training content has far outpaced the rise of mindset content when it comes to climbing. And they agree that climbing tends to be uniquely progress-oriented compared to other sports.

“It’s great to see the growth in top-end performance climbing, but for a lot of people, that might come with a lot of pressure to perform the same way,” says Louis Parkinson, the founder of the coaching company Catalyst Climbing, a climber of over 20 years, and co-author of the new book Get a Grip.

To write a self-help book for climbers focused exclusively on mindset, Parkinson teamed up with Joel Robertson, an MA MBACP psychotherapist and climber. Nicknamed “The Climbing Therapist,” Robertson insists that their book isn’t only for elite or performance-oriented athletes. That’s because he believes climbers at any level can experience the pressure and negative thought patterns that the sport can induce. He also sees negative mentality extending beyond the sport.

“If you’re being brutal to yourself at the crag or in the gym in ways that are holding you back in climbing, then you’re almost certainly doing that to yourself at family Christmas or at work or whatever,” Robertson says. “Mental health and climbing mindset are not separate, right? Let’s treat them the same. That’s the whole ethos of the book.”

Both Parkinson and Robertson admit that they are far from perfect when it comes to their own mentality. They emphasize that a healthy climbing mindset requires continuous work, rather than a one-time solution.

A former competitive climber, Parkinson recalls a period where he stopped enjoying climbing. This triggered an identity crisis of sorts, since he had oriented his entire life and career around the sport. “If I stop climbing, then I don’t know who I am,” Parkinson recalls thinking.

Eventually, Parkinson realized that his lack of enjoyment stemmed from the immense pressure he was putting on himself to continuously improve. When he couldn’t perform up to his own standards, he became “really, really upset.” Once he eased off the unrealistic expectations he was holding himself too, the joy came back. Parkinson’s past struggle echoes a similar experience of Chris Sharma. Earlier this year, he talked with Climbing about letting go of grades in order to send Biographie, the world’s first 5.15.

Robertson, primarily a casual indoor boulderer, shares a more recent experience from a couple weeks ago. After three sessions, he flashed his gym project. In the midst of some celebratory fist pumps, however, he watched in mild horror as someone else came and flashed his project as their warm-up. “It’s so classic,” Robertson says of this common climbing predicament. “I genuinely felt way less good about the achievement and not just the achievement, but myself.”

To avoid comparing yourself to others in a negative way, one suggestion Get a Grip offers is to think about your climbing friends. Do you love and value them because of their climbing ability, or because of who they are? Most people care about each of their friends as a person, not in terms of their climbing abilities. When you start to compare yourself to others, or base your self-worth on whether you, for example, sent your project, try to view yourself as you would your friend instead.

Robertson and Parkinson also suggest focusing on comparisons that are accurate and valuable, rather than grounded in envy or self-pity. Instead of thinking, “Damn, I wish I could climb like that,” ask, “What could I learn from watching someone else that I could apply in my own climbing?”

One of the critical ways to work on climbing mindset is to cultivate more awareness around our own thoughts, according to Robertson and Parkinson. Rather than becoming bogged down in the thought, attempt to view the thought impartially. Try reframing the thought, or compartmentalizing it. “Rather than ‘I am anxious,’ it’s ‘a part of me is anxious,’” Robertson explains. This can help you get some distance between yourself and a fleeting notion or emotion.

Throughout the book, reflections from pro climbers bring more color and insight to what a strong mindset looks like. In one of my favorite sections, British boulderer and competitive climber Shauna Coxsey talks about asking questions instead of making statements. An “exploratory mindset,” as Robertson and Parkinson term it, will fuel you with curiosity rather than pressure. “People often think I’m a very motivated person, but I would disagree,” Coxsey writes after sharing her focus on curiosity. “I think I’m a very committed person. For me, motivation and commitment have to go hand in hand because it’s impossible to be motivated all the time.”

Another standout pro mindset cameo comes from another British boulderer and comp climber: Hamish McArthur. Essentially, he reveals that he more or less blacks out when he climbs hard. This allows him to enter the coveted flow state that so many of us seek. “The times when I’ve performed at my best, I don’t really have any memory of what it was like,” he writes.

I took a lot away from the book in terms of how to edit and take control of my internal monologue. But I was left with one nagging question: How can we all climb more like McArthur, and find that elusive flow state?

“Just think less. It’s easy!” Parkinson joked with me. “No, it’s really hard. It’s insanely difficult.” Parkinson clarifies that achieving a mindset like McArthur’s requires a long-term commitment to honing your meditation skills so you can quiet your mind and just climb. But the lessons in Get a Grip can help get you started.

Vertebrate Publishing released Get a Grip on October 8. You can find a copy from Catalyst Climbing, Amazon, and wherever books are sold. Climbers can also listen to Get a Grip as an audiobook narrated by Parkinson.

#8216. Is an AI Data Center Coming for Your Favorite Trail? Check This Map and See

(Photo: Courtesy of More Than Just Parks)

As America grapples with the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence data centers, two brothers have set out to map infrastructure project proposals nationwide—including those near public lands and national parks.

Will Pattiz is the cofounder of More Than Just Parks, an independent public lands publication that tracks AI data centers. According to his research, at least 14 proposed data center projects are within ten miles of a national park boundary. His data also shows that 38 sites are planned within 25 miles of a national park, and 131 are within 50 miles.

“The basic idea is that a lot of these [projects] are being done under the cloak of darkness or secrecy, and we want folks to know where they’re coming in and who’s building them,” Pattiz, a resident of Portland, Oregon, told Outside. “The stance that we take is that we don’t want them on public lands.”

“Places like Utah, for example, have a huge amount of data center projects and some of the biggest ones that are being proposed,” Pattiz said. “Just depending on the size and scale, they take up a massive amount of resources and will have impacts on public lands one way or the other, whether it’s taking water or the land itself.”

Data centers are rapidly popping up across the United States, fueled by the computing needs of artificial intelligence and cloud-based software. These centers house massive servers, data storage systems, and networking equipment, and they require sizable amounts of electricity and water to run and maintain the hardware.

“The question that we want to see asked is: ‘What is the public benefit from this?’” Pattiz said. “So far, the ones that have been proposed on public lands, there’s no public benefit that’s been outlined.”

To use Pattiz’s map, a user inputs their zip code, and the site shows the closest data center or proposed facility. The site then suggests how the center will affect utility costs, as well as the groups that support the center.

“You can go through that discovery process yourself to decide whether you support [the center] or not, because these are things that are going to impact all of us, and you can decide where you land on that,” Pattiz said.

The map auto-populates as more information becomes available. As of this writing, the tool reflects 2,086 data centers, 741 of which are still in the proposal phase. Of those, 77 are located within ten miles of protected land like national parks, wildlife refuges, and wilderness or conservation areas. Roughly half are in the American West.

In Virginia, 97 data centers are proposed, and 12 are within 25 miles of Shenandoah National Park.

At least 25 data centers are proposed in Indiana, according to the map, and eight are located within 25 miles of Indiana Dunes National Park.

The map also includes several construction proposals that are extremely close to iconic National Park Service sites.

Arizona alone has 26 active proposals, with three within 25 miles of a national park. In January, the City of Page sold roughly 500 acres to developers planning to build a $10 billion data center next to Horseshoe Bend, an iconic viewpoint along the Colorado River. The 500-acre parcel was previously protected for outdoor recreation. According to the City of Page, the proposal is undergoing public review and has not yet been formally adopted, but a planning and zoning meeting is scheduled for November 17.

According to Pattiz’s map, the center is also located about five miles from the northeastern edge of Grand Canyon National Park near Lees Ferry.

Just outside of Price, Utah, Pattiz found that a company called Valar Atomics applied for more than 9,000 acres of Bureau of Land Management land for data center buildouts, including permits for hundreds of small nuclear reactors, a fuel plant, and nuclear waste storage.

According to a report published by NPR, the so-called Project Beehive would produce about 9.6 gigawatts of power for data centers. Currently, the entire state of Utah produces less than half of that on average, NPR reports.

The land is about two hours from both Arches and Canyonlands National Parks.

Located about 40 miles from Zion National Park, Antelope Data Center is slated for development as part of a 640-acre, 1.5-gigawatt project that will include an on-site natural gas power plant, according to The Salt Lake Tribune. The Iron County Commission approved a conditional use permit in June 2026.

Large-scale data center rollouts represent an inflection point in American history, Pattiz said. As construction crews have erected these centers, they have become political lightning rods in American towns and cities.

Pattiz believes that giving Americans transparent, readily available information about where big tech is breaking ground will help them track what developers are building in their backyards.

“At the end of the day, data is data,” he added. “Whether or not there’s a need for these things is a totally separate question from where they’re being built and what impact they’re going to have on you and the places that you love.”

#8215. Escape Winter With These 6 Underrated Desert Trail Runs

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

In his research for his upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” Andy Cochrane ran hundreds of trails across the U.S. These are his six favorites across the Southwest that come into season when most of the country is hibernating.

With all due respect to Presidential Traverse, Teton Crest, and Wonderland, the most sought-after one-day trail running route in the U.S. is the Grand Canyon Rim-to-Rim-to-Rim. Every spring and fall runners flock to Arizona to test their luck on this double lap of the big ditch, despite the National Park Service strongly advising against it. (Signs around the Grand Canyon warn of heat illness, elevation, and difficult evacs.)

Some have called R2R2R an obsession—while I’m not sure I would personally go that far, I do see the argument. I’ve run the route three times and each trip I find myself more enamored than the last. On my last visit in 2023, a peak autumn weekend with nearly perfect temps and all the water facets still running (the NPS shuts some of them down seasonally), I saw hundreds of runners attempting R2R2R. That’s a tiny fraction of the four and a half million people who visit the park each year, but very busy for a trail run.

However, that was before the closures. The North Rim of the Grand Canyon was shuttered for most of the 2025 season due to the Dragon Bravo Fire, which burned 149,000 acres and 118 buildings. Then, on August 29th, 2026, a flash flood struck Phantom Ranch at the bottom of the Grand Canyon, killing three and forcing 82 others to be evacuated by helicopter. Trail damage was widespread, taking out footbridges and much of the park’s water line. The North Kaibab Trail, parts of the Bright Angel and South Kaibab trails, and sections of the River Trail remain closed with no set date for reopening.

It’s getting colder and darker across most of the country. That means one thing: It’s desert season. In lieu of a double dip into the Grand Canyon—and to open your mind to the endless possibilities elsewhere—I’ve compiled a list of my six favorite trails across the American Southwest. All of them are in my upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” (which you can pre-order now!). They cover six different states and four unique desert ecosystems, so there is plenty of variety to choose from.

Unlike the rocky singletrack of the Northeast, the forested trails of the upper Midwest, or the alpine ridges of the West, running across the Southwest desert is a singular experience. Limited shade, even less water, and direct solar radiation create obvious hydration challenges. The temperature swings dramatically from near freezing overnight to scorching heat midday. The trails themselves are a mix of surfaces, from soft sand to loose scree to firm slickrock, with many—including the ones listed below—being very remote.

Beyond the physical experience, running in arid environments carries a different emotion, too. I often find myself in a quiet and contemplative mental space, passing by ancient saguaros, joshua trees, and prickly pears while trying to stay alert for subtle movements of rattlesnakes, lizards, and coyotes. Running in the desert is, simultaneously, the antidote to life’s complexity and a plague of endless possibility.

There are four distinct desert ecosystems in the U.S. The northernmost is the Great Basin, which covers most of Nevada and parts of neighboring states, making it the largest desert in the country. With frigid winters, it’s filled with sagebrush instead of cacti. Just south is the Mojave, the smallest of the four, which is home to Death Valley and Joshua Tree. Further south is the Sonoran, the “green desert,” with large saguaros and rainfall in both summer and winter. Last, the Chihuahuan, covers West Texas and southern New Mexico, and is known for succulents like Agave, Yucca, and Creosote.

Hidden in one of North America’s most remote national parks, Big Bend, the Outer Mountain Loop is a 32-mile circuit featuring a stark ecological contrast between the Chihuahuan Desert and the high-alpine Chisos Mountains. Beginning and ending in the Chisos Basin, a sky-island that’s home to rare species like the Colima Warbler, the trail plunges down stone steps and rolls across the sun-scorched flats of the Dodson Trail before making a grueling 3,000-foot final ascent up Blue Creek Canyon. Early Spanish explorers called this isolated region El Despoblado.

Why I love it: Getting to experience both sky islands and the solitude of the Chihuahuan desert.

Spanning 39 miles from the edge of the Navajo Nation to the Grand Canyon’s South Rim, the Little to Big Colorado route is the less conventional way to explore one of the country’s most popular national parks. Tracing the historic Hopi salt journeys, the route plunges down Bekihatso Wash, follows the Little Colorado to its confluence with the Colorado River, passes sacred sites, scrambles obstacles like the Papago Wall, and passes by billion-year-old rock. With a 4,700-foot grind up the New Hance Trail at the end, it’s just as challenging and rewarding as rim-to-rim-to-rim.

Why I love it: It’s so close to the most famous one day trail route in the country, but still unheard of.

Crossing the national park from east to west, this 37-mile rolling route passes two distinct deserts—the higher Mojave and the lower Sonora—as you wander by long shadows of Yucca brevifolia (Joshua trees) and massive, weathered granite batholiths. Championed by the activist Minerva Hamilton Hoyt after decades of cattle grazing and mining exploitation, this sandy sanctuary strips away the crowds, offering sheer solitude as runners cross ancient mountain passes, gaze down at the dark expanse of the Salton Sea, and experience a desert communion.

Why I love it: it’s the one place in America that feels straight out of a Dr. Seuss book.

One of the most remote routes we considered for the book, this 64-mile trek traces the ridgeline of the Toiyabe Range. Like Outer Mountain, this area is a sky island, a rare ecosystem in which the valley below is a scorching hot desert, but the trail itself is a lush forest of aspen and bristlecone pines, some 3,000 years old. Despite being Nevada’s longest named trail, Toiyabe is off-trail in nature, with significant routefinding and some sections of unrunnable terrain.

Why I love it: Remote and rugged, it’s a good test of navigation and alpine movement of all sorts.

Perched above Albuquerque, this 26-mile trail follows a limestone ridge along the backbone of the Sandia Mountains, with 360-degree views of the Rio Grande Valley below. Sandia is Spanish for watermelon, named after the ridge’s unique sunset alpenglow that turns the cliffs deep pink, with green conifers on top representing the rind. The trail features wildflowers, ponderosas, spruce, and white fir, and can be accessed via an aerial tramway, providing easy access without sacrificing its rugged, aesthetic appeal.

Why I love it: Quick and easy access paired with absolutely beautiful sunsets.

Winding through one of Southern Utah’s most distinctive landscapes, the 30-mile Bryce Canyon Traverse links the heavily trafficked northern amphitheater where thousands of hoodoos, rock fins, and natural arches create a natural maze with the primitive Under the Rim Trail to the south. Crossing a geological marvel shaped by erosion and freeze-thaw cycles over millions of years, the traverse is the best way to see it all. Heading southbound allows runners to catch sunrise over the spires before descending into remote backcountry, which is the direction we recommend.

Why I love it: There’s no place in the world with the same density or volume of hoodoos.

Desert running presents many challenges that the Mafate X can handle. Deserts are often oven-hot, so having a woven, high-airflow upper is ideal. They are rocky and filled with pokey things, so having a taller stack with soft PEBA foam is a bonus. They are loose, so having Vibram lugs adds a level of stability and confidence. And, with uneven ground, a wide base makes your feet feel much more planted, too.

On long, sweaty days, sunscreen only goes so far. I take extra precaution and wear a Tahoe sun hoody, which delivers UPF 50+ protection against harsh UV rays, paired with a light polyester-spandex knit that wicks sweat off my skin and dries quickly. And, integrated thumbholes and a fitted hood keep my hands and neck completely covered without restricting movement.

For most desert runs I recommend stashing water the day before, but if you aren’t able to, having an extra large running pack is key. Kiprun’s 10L has room for a bladder in the back and two flasks up front, which is ideal for long desert stretches. The harness keeps the pack secure and large front pockets make it easy to access your phone, electrolytes, snacks, or sunscreen on the go.

My favorite drink mix, Fuel combines essential electrolytes like sodium, potassium, and magnesium to replace minerals lost in heavy sweat. It tastes good, prevents cramps, and the added zinc supports fluid retention in hot conditions. Using a low-GI carb from beet sugar, it also provides steady energy without blood sugar spikes or crashes, which is great for longer days.

#8213. Shah Daulat, a Celebrated Alpinist Who Summited K2, Dies at 31

Shah Daulat, 31, was raised in the mountains of Shimshal, a remote village in Pakistan’s Hunza Valley that has encouraged and supported generations of the country’s strongest climbers. In his early years of being a professional guide with the Karakoram Mountain Guides Association, Daulat climbed four of the world’s 8,000-meter peaks, cementing his legacy as one of Pakistan’s rising alpinists.

“His journey from a mountain guide to climbing some of the world’s most challenging peaks is something our family is incredibly proud of,” Ibadat said. “He dedicated his life to the mountains and was deeply passionate about climbing.”

Daulat began working as a guide in 2022, and his progression onto the world’s highest peaks came quickly. That year, he summited K2, at 8,611 meters the second-highest mountain in the world. In 2023, he climbed 8,126-meter Nanga Parbat without supplemental oxygen, followed by Gasherbrum II in 2024. In 2025, he summited Gasherbrum I, again without supplemental oxygen, marking his fourth 8,000-meter summit in as many years. That same year, he also climbed Laila Peak, a 6,096-meter mountain in Pakistan’s Hushe Valley.

But his life in the mountains extended far beyond expedition climbing. He was a skier, too, competing at Malam Jabba in northern Pakistan in 2022. And though his career took him to some of the highest vistas in the world, it was on a much smaller objective, close to home, that he passed.

On February 6, 2026, Daulat was ice climbing near Khyber village in Gojal, Hunza, when he fell nearly 400 meters. Local volunteers recovered his body, which was later returned to his home village of Shimshal for burial.

After his death, Daulat’s cousin, pioneering Pakistani mountaineer Samina Baig, remembered both what he had accomplished in a remarkably short climbing career and the person behind those achievements. “Shah Daulat was a true gem in our family—a cherished younger brother (cousin) taken from us far too soon,” Baig wrote in a Facebook tribute. “A young mountaineer, he achieved so much in such a short life, touching many hearts with his courage and gentle spirit.

“May he rest in peace among the mountains he loved,” she continued. “He will forever remain in our hearts, remembered with love and quiet pride.”

In September, the villages of Shimsal and Khyber jointly installed a life-sized memorial sculpture of Daulat near the Khyber Ice Wall, which has been renamed the Shah Daulat Ice Wall.

#8212. “These Aren’t Victimless Crimes.” Vandals Deface Ancient Petroglyphs Near Moab.

Vandals scratched graffiti above ancient animal petroglyphs at the Bear Panel along Highway 279 near Moab, Utah. (Photo: BLM Utah)

The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) announced on November 6 that it was investigating vandalism at two ancient rock-art sites near Moab, Utah, where someone carved names into petroglyphs, leaving damage that may be impossible to remove.

The incidents occurred at the Bear Panel, a rock-art site along Highway 279 near the Colorado River, and another panel near Hell’s Revenge, a popular four-wheel-drive trail in the Sand Flats Recreation Area.

“These images are a physical expression of the past, their connection to their ancestors and to that landscape,” Chris Merritt, Utah’s state historic preservation officer, told Outside. “They will now forever be scarred by someone’s thoughtlessness, and that hurts the continuation of culture.”

The BLM has not publicly identified any suspects in the two latest incidents. An agency spokesperson told the Moab newspaper The Times-Independent that the agency planned to treat the graffiti in the days following its November 6 announcement, although some damage may be permanent.

Under the federal Archaeological Resources Protection Act, vandalizing protected archaeological sites can carry fines of up to $20,000 and two years in prison.

Photos show the name “Meru” scratched beside ancient carvings depicting a bear and a bighorn sheep at the Bear Panel. At the second site, near Hell’s Revenge, someone carved “Craig W” across several petroglyph figures.

Merritt said much of the artwork at the two sites dates back roughly 1,500 years and reflects Ancestral Puebloan and Fremont traditions, along with those of more recent Indigenous communities. The panels are part of a larger cultural landscape around Moab, where Indigenous peoples once lived, farmed, and traveled, he said.

Restoring the damaged petroglyphs presents different challenges at each site, Merritt said.

At the site near Hell’s Revenge, vandals scratched graffiti directly across ancient carvings. Merritt noted that typical fixes, such as scrubbing the stone or trying to conceal the marks with pigments, risk damaging the original artwork underneath.

The Bear Panel presents a different problem. A crack in the sandstone just below the graffiti means that scraping the rock could create openings for rainwater, weakening the structure through freeze-thaw cycles.

“Five minutes of damage could take weeks of repair to do carefully to preserve the subsurface imagery and the rock face,” Merritt said, emphasizing that any remediation must involve consultation with descendant tribal communities.

Merritt said rock-art vandalism has become more widespread in Utah in recent years, a problem he believes is partly connected to growing visitation on public lands.

“We’ve always had folks going back to the 19th century scraping their initials on the panels, but what we’re seeing within five or six years is a pretty significant increase in the scale and distribution, hitting archaeological panels that have never had graffiti before,” Merritt said.

The latest incidents follow another case in March 2026, when the Grand County Sheriff’s Office investigated graffiti carved into petroglyphs near Tusher Tunnel, along an off-highway vehicle route northwest of Moab.

To combat the problem, Merritt said Utah is using its Protect Our Past education campaign and a statewide network of volunteer site stewards who monitor archaeological sites. Signage and fencing can also help discourage vandalism, he said.

In November 2025, a Utah woman who vandalized petroglyphs on BLM land near Wire Pass was sentenced to 12 months of probation and ordered to pay $14,853 in fines and restitution, according to a U.S. Department of Justice news release. She was also prohibited from entering BLM land during her probation.

“These aren’t victimless crimes,” Merritt said. “We need to find ways to catch, prosecute, and convict these folks, so it sends a message to future visitors that this is not acceptable in Utah or anywhere you visit heritage sites.”

Anyone with information is asked to contact Moab BLM Law Enforcement at 435-259-2131.

The fit is a bit baggy for the ultralight crowd, but the oversized silhouette is modern and slick. Five stars—a perfect holiday gift for any outdoorsy (or outdoorsy-ish) person on your list. REI Co-op members get 20% off with coupon HOLIDAY2026.

There are certain things I strongly believe you should splurge on. Snowboards, for instance. You get what you pay for there. But other gear categories, like base layers, you can often get away with a more affordable option. REI Co-op base layers fall into the latter category. That said, I’d recommend skipping the synthetics and stepping up to REI’s 100-percent merino base layers. Merino’s a natural fiber with intrinsic warmth and wicking properties, plus antimicrobial magic for hut trips and multi-day ski road trips. Yes, REI’s merino options are pricier than the Co-op synthetics, but they’re also significantly cheaper than pure merino base layers from the competition—especially during REI’s holiday sale.

I’ve relied on Thule RoundTrip snowboard bags on multiple international shred missions over the years, from road trips through British Columbia’s Powder Highway to train-hopping around the Alps. Fat rolling wheels, easy-grab handles, and ample padding and protection make these Thule ski and snowboard bags an easy recommendation, even at full retail. However, all Thule ski and snowboard bags are currently 25 percent off. Skiers will be stoked to note that tester-approved RoundTrip boot bags are similarly on sale. And snowboarders will be stoked to note that they don’t need a boot bag.

The Car Seat Towel is basically just a regular quick-drying Nomadix towel, with a small hood that slips over your car headrest. It doesn’t secure tightly to your car seat like a designated seat cover, but it works well enough on the road. I just put it to the test on a three-week road trip to the Tetons and had no complaints in that department. The real beauty is that it doubles as a proper towel, too, so you can dry off after impromptu swims, surfs, you name it. On that Teton road trip, the Car Seat Towel was a day-saver after the muddiest day of fly-fishing of my life. Apart from the ski socks you’ll find below, this is also the most affordable pick in this article, and a gift that any self-respecting (and rig-respecting) road tripper will dig.

There’s no piece of gear in this article—hell, in the entirety of that 7000+ product REI sale—that I use more than the AeroPress Steel. (Once daily, twice if I’m on deadline, three times if I’m looking longingly at that deadline in my rearview mirror.) If you already have an AeroPress that you know and love, this uses the same plunging pressure to yield a velvety cup of coffee. However, the AeroPress Steel ditches the plastic for a bomber, stainless steel body that I’m pretty sure I could run over with my Subaru. In fact, I just might run it over with my Subaru, for the sake of science, knowing that it’s now on sale for $119 at REI.

I’ve recommended the Smith Squad MAG more times than I can count. (I’m not a math guy, remember?) The lens interchangeability system balances the speed of magnets with the security of a locking mechanism, style is through the roof, and the lenses themselves are high-quality and offer excellent contrast and definition on the hill. If you’re unsure what to nab a skier or snowboarder for the holidays, my advice is always a pair of goggles. Lenses get scratched or lost easily, and any powderhound will appreciate an optical refresh.

If you replaced virtually all of my closet with Roark duds (technical outerwear aside), I’d be quite content. I’d also be quite stylish. And my wife would be quite content, too. Peep the Roark lineup here for suave men’s and women’s adventure wear, all discounted by 25 percent. Or, take a gander at my personal Roark go-to: the Bless Up Trail Shirt. An ultralight travel shirt that’s breathable enough for desert backpacking yet snazzy enough for summer nights on the town, this is a staple for me on any warm-weather trip. It’s also so packable that it would make a killer stocking stuffer!

Whether you’re in the market for a featherweight backpacking bag like the Spark, a lofty quilt like the Ember for fast-and-light alpine missions, or a cozy and wearable sleeping bag like the Trek, Sea to Summit’s got you covered. Well-designed, built to last, and currently on sale for 25 percent off—that’s a combo that’ll help any camper sleep soundly.

Stuffing Smartwool ski socks in a stocking is Inception-level gifting. It’s a sock—in a sock! It’s also an incredibly practical gift that any skier or snowboarder will appreciate immensely when the mercury drops, the powder falls, and the Sock Monster has swallowed up mate after mate, leaving behind a rag-tag collection of singles in the sock drawer. Of course, the sock monster is inevitable, his lust for lint unslakable. Eventually, these Smartwool socks, no matter how smart they really are, will be hunted, measured, and tasted by this Dark Lord of Laundry. #8210. The Sun Never Shines in This Norwegian Ice Climbing Mecca

Heike Schmitt leads the crux pitch of ‘Juvsøyla’ (WI5/6), one of Rjukan’s crown jewels. (Photo: Jonas Paulsson)

Norway in February is a lot like what you’d expect. Snow and ice-covered roads. Short, cold days. Long, cold nights. Endless forested mountains with sharply serrated interludes.

But I did not expect there to be so much ice.

In Rjukan, a town of 3,000 located three hours from the capital of Oslo, there are over 200 ice and mixed routes, up to 800 meters long, ranging from mellow WI2 flows to some of the hardest pure ice in Europe. Many of the routes are multi-pitch, and many can be accessed within 10 minutes of walking from your car.

As someone who lives in the ice mecca of the Canadian Rockies, I thought I’d seen what a “high concentration” of ice means. But drive through the tight, shaded valley of Rjukan in February and you’ll kink your neck eight ways at once trying to glimpse all the ice available to you. Crucially, there is a nearly endless supply of ice for beginners and intermediates—a WI2-4 climber’s delight.

I visited Rjukan in February 2025 to attend the Norrøna Ice Festival. Climbers from all over came to sample this world-class area—Italy, Poland, the United States, Scotland—and the Europeans in particular remarked at how reliable Norwegian ice seemed to be relative to the rest of the continent. It makes sense: Norway is famously cold, famously wet, and, for roughly half the year, the town of Rjukan sees exactly zero direct sunlight. That is a sure-fire recipe for fantastic ice climbing.

If you yearn to feel some sunlight on your face, drop in to the Rjukan town square on a clear day. In 2013, the municipality installed three giant mirrors on the north side of the valley, which are powered by solar and rotate to reflect the sun’s rays down into town.

I’ve been to a number of climbing festivals over the years—from Squamish to Spain, New Hampshire to Norway—and I found the Norrøna fest to be refreshingly unique. Rjukan is a bit of a backwoods town and just getting there is a minor hassle—especially for the many participants who are internationals and fly into Oslo. As a result, Norrøna offers a “full package” festival experience. The organizers told me and every other participant how to get from our arrival gates to their head office, fed us a three-course dinner, and let us climb at their gym (which rivals any mega gym I’ve ever visited), before schlepping us to Rjukan.

The “package” is certainly more expensive that bussing from Oslo, sleeping in a tent, and walking to each crag day after day, but, as one of the participants living in Italy pointed out to me, Norway is an expensive country to visit and organizing your own rental car, accommodation, and meals will shake out to nearly the same cost without the festival’s group rate. And, personally, I loved the camaraderie that developed between participants day after day, meal after meal.

Whether you’re considering visiting the Norrøna Ice Festival next year or just want to go experience this dark and dreamy valley of ice yourself, here are some tips I picked up from my trip.

Norway’s high-flow waterfalls, or fossen, are a sight to behold. But be warned, as I was by pro climber Matthias Scherer: these wet lines can be an absolute nightmare to descend, since freezing conditions will turn rappel ropes into thick, icy cables. Make sure to bring ropes with a fresh dry treatment.

#8209. The 10 Best Gifts for Ultralight Hikers in 2026

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Alpenglow Gear Alpenflow Fuel Transfer Valve

Hoping to buy a gift for an ultralight hiker? Here’s the hard truth: Whatever you purchase will be weighed, then quietly stuffed in a closet. I know, because after a decade of thru-hiking, I’ve almost completely wallpapered my small room with all the copies of Wild I’ve been given. Thank you, but please stop.

Apart from heavy gifts, the last thing an ultralight hiker needs is someone else choosing their big three. The little things, though? That’s where a good gift can surprise them. This year’s picks tackle ten small annoyances of life on trail, from a rigid bottle that actually works with a filter to a sun glove that doesn’t plaster to your hands.

Single-use bottles crease, crinkle, and need replacing, but my original ThruBottle survived 1,800 miles this summer with plenty of life left. My only gripe was that it was too stiff to squeeze water through a filter. I’ve upgraded to the new ThruBottle 1000, which has a softer body and sheds nearly an ounce, weighing 2.2 ounces for a full liter.

The zip-lock bag you’d rather no one ever rummaged through has a 0.14-ounce alternative: this cap turns a compatible 28 mm bottle into a portable bidet. I find that it works best with a squeezable bottle. Unlike TP, it never runs out halfway through a section.

I sleep cold, and when the temperature drops on the trail, my ears and neck are often the first places I want extra warmth. The Shag Hood, made from Polartec Alpha Direct, covers them for 1.16 ounces, so I can skip carrying another full layer. Bonus: It’s gorpcore enough to wear off trail too.

My old half-finger sun gloves always came off inside out, and getting them back on over sweaty hands was a nightmare. The éclipse gloves have a thumb hole and mitten-style opening, so they slide on and off. They weigh 0.35 ounces and give me UPF 50+ sun protection on the backs of my hands, where multiple rounds of sunscreen have never been enough.

A camera buried in your pack takes no photos. The three-ounce Capture Clip attaches to a shoulder strap or belt, so I can grab my camera when the light is just right, instead of getting stuck crouching over my pack, still fumbling for it when the light’s gone.

The long handle keeps your knuckles out of dinner at the bottom of a freeze-dried meal bag. The 0.8-ounce titanium spork would outlast my hiking career if I could stop losing it. I found four on my last thru-hike, so I’m clearly not the only one.

A half-empty fuel canister is too precious to toss but annoying to carry. I’ve envied hikers using heavier transfer valves, but couldn’t justify the weight until the Alpenflow dropped. It weighs 0.09 ounces and transfers leftover fuel between two standard EN417 canisters, including those from MSR, Jetboil, and Snow Peak.

Leukotape is my holy grail bandage. It stays on through sweat, mud, and sketchy river crossings, and I’ve accidentally left a strip on for weeks. It’s gotten harder for me to find it in stores lately, so a spare roll is a keeper. I wrap a generous amount around my trekking poles instead of carrying the full 3.9-ounce roll.

For 10,000 thru-hiking miles, my pillow was the head of my dirty air mattress propped up on a water bottle, which rolled out from under me all night. Don’t make my mistake. For 1.9 ounces, the regular size is the real deal, and it packs down to the size of a pool ball. Pricey for a pillow, but I sleep better.

This 0.11-ounce Dyneema pouch stops loose tent stakes from rattling around in your pack. You don’t think you need one until a rogue stake starts working its way through your bug netting. Not that I, a seasoned professional and expert patcher, know anything about that.

#8208. Rescuers Carried a 105-Pound Labrador down a Steep Virginia Mountain after Two Days

Rescuers administer fluids to Archie, a nine-year-old Labrador retriever, after carrying him down a steep Virginia mountainside on November 11. The dog had been missing for two days before searchers located him by following his howls. (Photo: Angels of Assisi)

When Roanoke County’s technical rescue teams were called to a steep Virginia mountainside on November 11, the stranded subject wasn’t a hiker or climber. It was Archie, a 105-pound yellow Labrador Retriever who had been missing for two days.

The nine-year-old dog disappeared on November 9 while his owner was hiking in the Bent Mountain area, according to Facebook updates from Angels of Assisi, a Roanoke animal welfare organization. After searchers located the dog by following his howls, firefighters from three stations helped carry Archie down the mountainside in a specialized rescue stretcher.

Basit Jimoh, lead surgical assistant at Angels of Assisi, told Outside he joined the search on November 10 after learning that Archie was missing. According to Jimoh, searchers deployed drones in the area that evening, hoping to spot Archie from above, but turned up nothing.

The following afternoon, officials received reports from people hearing a dog whining on the steep, wooded mountainside. With the leaf-covered slope too slick to descend safely from above, Jimoh approached from the bottom, calling Archie’s name and listening for his howls to guide him uphill.

“I had a horse-leading halter and wrapped that around myself,” Jimoh said. “I started climbing, and whenever there was a tree close by, I’d wrap it around the tree and use it to pull myself up.”

Eventually, Jimoh found Archie lying in a ditch beneath a fallen tree.

“When he first saw somebody after being stuck in that ditch for two days, he was really excited,” Jimoh said. “He was wagging his tail. You could tell he was really, really tired, but he was really happy.”

Jimoh and other rescuers suspect Archie slipped and tumbled down the mountainside, although nobody witnessed his fall. The dog was exhausted and managed to stand only briefly after being helped out of the ditch.

Finding Archie was one thing.  Getting him down the mountain was another.

“The problem with Archie was that he is about 105 pounds,” Jimoh said. “He’s not a small guy.”

With that much weight to maneuver down a steep, slippery, leaf-covered slope, Jimoh tried using the same horse halter he’d relied on to climb uphill. But before he could get Archie to safety, Roanoke County Fire and Rescue crews arrived and advised that the route he was taking led toward a dangerous drop-off. Instead, rescuers located an old logging trail that offered a safer route down.

The steep, rocky terrain was difficult to navigate without specialized equipment, Roanoke County Fire and Rescue Captain John Richardson told Outside.

Using ropes and a rigging system, firefighters lowered Archie approximately 80 feet down the mountainside. They then placed him in a rescue sled and carried him out to safety. Richardson said 13 rescuers participated in the operation, including four who carried Archie out.

Once they reached the bottom, Jimoh administered fluids before transporting Archie to Angels of Assisi for treatment. Veterinary staff performed blood work and X-rays and provided additional fluids, pain medication, and antibiotics. Jimoh said Archie suffered scrapes and bruising but had no broken bones. He has since returned home to his family.

For Jimoh, Archie’s ordeal is a reminder that even well-trained dogs can get into trouble when exploring unfamiliar terrain.

“I know a lot of people think their animals’ recall skills are great, but sometimes they’re just excited to be out,” Jimoh said. “They want to sniff everything. They want to go everywhere. You never know.”

The American Hiking Society recommends keeping dogs leashed on hikes to prevent them from wandering out of sight, particularly important when trails run near dangerous terrain. Jimoh also recommends attaching a tracking device to a dog’s collar, which he believes could have made finding Archie much easier.

#8207. The Ephemeral Global Climbing School Amid China’s Epic Limestone

On October 22, hundreds of climbers of all skill levels descended upon Yangshuo, China, for the long-awaited  2026 Arc’teryx Climb Academy. Participants say the remarkable thing about the weekend wasn’t just the climbing or even the new skills they learned—it was the magic of the remote, fantastical landscape, and the opportunity to connect with people across cultures and continents.

The Arc’teryx Climb Academy is a roving international climbing school—and one that offers some of the most advanced mountain education in the world. Since 2007, academies have been held in global climbing epicenters like Squamish, Chamonix, and Mammoth Lakes. Some focus on climbing while others offer backcountry or freeride skiing education. Each installment is a complex undertaking, bringing together world-class guides and athletes to pass on their knowledge in a highly efficient, structured format. Dozens of courses—ranging from alpine overnights to big wall workshops to mental resilience clinics—are designed to meet participants where they’re at. At each academy, students can learn skills from scratch, drill fundamentals, or significantly boost their skills, even within just a few days of instruction.

While there are tons of events in the climbing universe, Arc’teryx Climb Academies stand out for just how seamlessly they’re run and how well integrated they are into the local community. Unlike some climbing festivals, which tend to put more emphasis on socialization than education, Arc’teryx has figured out how to nail both without compromising either. All day long, participants of every skill level take hands-on courses on some of the best rock in the world, each one packed with pro-level hacks, technique drills, and actionable tips for continuing your education after the trip ends. Each evening, a five-star lineup of films, speakers, music, and parties makes it impossible to tear yourself away. Every chapter of the event buoys you along to the next. The weekend passes in a flash. And you return home with more phone numbers, more new climbing partners, and more stoke than you could have imagined possible.

In 2023, the series brought this special blend of inspiration and education to the limestone cliffs of Yangshuo, China—and the event was a runaway hit. In 2024, the Academy returned with even more courses crafted specifically for the local community, including rescue and evacuation clinics tailored to China’s uniquely rocky landscapes. The 2026 Academy further expanded the course menu, offering beginner trad clinics, bolting workshops, and masterclasses in big wall climbing. Over four days, hundreds of climbers participated in 37 clinics at more than a dozen crags across the stunning Guangxi region. It was the region’s biggest Arc’teryx Climb Academy yet.

While many of the Academy’s participants came specifically to experience Yangshuo’s world-renowned karst spires, the crags aren’t just a backdrop here; they’re the heart of a thriving and longstanding community of climbers, route developers, and outdoor businesses. Since international climbers first arrived in the late 1980s, the zone has grown to nearly 2,000 routes across 74 crags on world-class limestone.

“Yangshuo means a lot to me,” says Peng Zhou, renowned Chinese mountaineer and Arc’teryx athlete. “I completed both my first 5.12 and 5.14 routes here, and it has left me with many wonderful memories.” He loves getting an opportunity to share this place with newcomers; it’s one of the reasons he comes back to teach year after year.

Given Yangshuo’s robust existing climbing scene, the event offers more cultural exchange than top-down discourse. Here, international visitors learn just as much from their Chinese counterparts as locals learn from the global pros.

Take it from Arc’teryx athlete Quentin Roberts. This year, he taught his third Yangshuo Big Wall Climbing clinic in a row. Each time, he’s astonished by how much the climbing community has grown since his last visit. “Every year I feel like I have had to level up to meet the growing ambitions and skills of the participants,” he says. “It’s exciting to see how eager everyone is.”

But for Roberts, the best part about climbing in China is the profound and indescribable warmth of the Yangshuo community.

“We always have a big, Chinese-style, round-table dinner with all the instructors before the event,” he says. It’s an evening filled with laughter between old friends. Jokes and stories fly across the table like sparks, and Roberts leaves feeling filled up at a soul level. “Many of the people in that room are at the forefront of climbing in China. It’s special to feel that sense of family, and to see the passion everyone has for what they’re doing.”

It’s that sense of connection that makes the Yangshuo event—and the other installments of the Arc’teryx Climb Academy—so invaluable.

“Coming to China over the years and connecting with people through climbing has really reinforced something I believe deeply: we are all more similar than we are different,” says Roberts. “Climbing has an incredible ability to bring people together. Sharing a rope, trusting one another, sharing our experiences—those connections transcend language and culture.”

Arc’teryx is a Canadian company based in the Coast Mountains. Our design process is connected to the real world, focused on delivering unrivaled durability and performance in extreme conditions. Our products are distributed through over 160 branded stores and more than 2,400 retail locations worldwide. We are problem solvers, evolving and searching for a better way to deliver resolved, minimalist designs. Good design that matters makes lives better.

#8201. This Favorite Trail Shoe Just Got a Thru-Hiking Upgrade

Topo Athletic's new Traverse 2. (Photo: Topo Athletic)

It’s a toss-up what thru-hikers think about more: food, or their feet. After all, when you’re on the trail hour after hour, day after day, you can’t replenish calories fast enough. And at that pace, small flaws in shoe design can quickly magnify into a full-blown sufferfest. But with the right footwear—a shoe that provides the perfect combination of stability, durability, and comfort—thru-hikers can stop worrying about their feet and get on with daydreaming about their next cheeseburger.

Thru-hikers have already discovered Topo Athletic’s Traverse low-top hiking shoe, and appreciate its traction, toughness, and tailored fit on the longest trails. The latest iteration, the Traverse 2, builds on that foundation with new details geared specifically to multi-month objectives like the Appalachian Trail and Pacific Crest Trail.

Extended adventures demand durability, so the Traverse 2 features a new, high-abrasion mesh upper with strategically placed overlays that fend off trail debris without adding extra ounces (which is key when deciding what is and isn’t worth the weight on lengthy thru hikes). Protecting feet from dirt, rocks, and precipitation is also essential for logging long trail miles day after day, so Topo Athletic added its universal gaiter attachment system to the Traverse 2.

The Traverse 2 is built for anything the terrain throws at you. The full-length Vibram ® Megagrip outsole digs into technical, rocky, and wet trails, while a flexible forefoot rock plate beefs up underfoot protection. The three-piece midsole platform is designed for all-day hiking with a heavy pack, with a softer foam on the base of the heel and a firmer foam on the medial arch for maximum stability. Topo Athletic’s FKT insole features TPU beads not only for rebound and comfort, but also to help the shoes drain and dry in a flash. The shoe’s 5-millimeter drop hits the sweet spot to provide a more natural gait across long distances. And of course, the brand’s signature fit combines a roomy toe box with a snug fit around the midfoot and heel for a naturally comfortable feel.

All this comes in a streamlined package that keeps you light on your feet. The Traverse 2 weighs in at 9.2 ounces for a women’s 7 and 11.2 ounces for a men’s 9. It’s the kind of shoe that lets thru-hikers forget about their feet and focus on the adventure (or visions of that next cheeseburger).

Topo Athletic, based in Framingham, Massachusetts, empowers people to move better for life. Rooted in the belief that every step shapes the journey, Topo builds performance-driven footwear with a focus on lasting comfort and durability, all with its signature fit.

#8196. A Teen Rescuer Helped Save a Lost Senior Hiker with FaceTime Tech Support

Marin County Search and Rescue volunteers escort an 88-year-old hiker through Mount Burdell Preserve in Northern California after locating her on November 10 with help from a teenage volunteer who used FaceTime to retrieve her GPS coordinates. (Photo: Marin County Search and Rescue)

A 17-year-old search-and-rescue volunteer helped locate a lost 88-year-old hiker in Northern California after conventional cellphone-tracking methods failed.

The volunteer rescuer, named Cody Davis, eventually used FaceTime to take control of the hiker’s iPhone screen and retrieve her GPS coordinates.

“I’m not a super tech person,” Davis told Outside. “But I’m young, and it’s easy for us to figure stuff like that out.”

The woman was found uninjured on November 10 at Mount Burdell Preserve, near Novato, California, after becoming separated from her hiking companions. Molly Williams, operations director for Marin County Search and Rescue, told Outside that the woman had gotten off the trail and headed downhill, although it remains unclear how the separation happened. Her companions tried unsuccessfully to locate her before calling for help.

Around 50 members of Marin County Search and Rescue mobilized to search the preserve. Williams, who oversaw the operation, said rescuers received the call around 2 P.M. and located the woman around 4 P.M.

A report of the rescue mission was published on the Marin County Search and Rescue group’s Facebook page.

Davis, a high school senior, was among the first search and rescue volunteers to arrive on the scene. According to Williams, Marin County’s search-and-rescue team accepts volunteers as young as 14.

“Probably a third or more of our members are high school age, and they are full members,” Williams said. “They respond in the same ways as the adults.”

Before rescuers arrived, 911 dispatchers had also tried and failed to pinpoint the missing hiker’s position by phone. When Davis got to the command post, he called her to ask about her surroundings, but Mount Burdell’s rolling hills and scattered trees offered few distinguishing landmarks. Attempts to track her through CalTopo, a search-and-rescue mapping platform, and Apple’s Find My Friends feature were also unsuccessful.

Davis eventually connected with the woman over FaceTime and asked her to show him the terrain. When that didn’t help, he remembered hearing that newer versions of FaceTime allowed users to remotely control another person’s iPhone screen with permission.

“I was able to remotely access her screen, which was weird,” Davis told Outside. “I’d never done that before, but I just sorta figured it out.”

At that point, Davis had already spent roughly an hour and a half on the phone with the hiker, he told Outside. Their calls kept dropping, and although the woman was unfamiliar with some of her phone’s features, she worked with Davis as he patiently explained each step.

“She was great, and was as helpful as she could be, being unfamiliar with the device,” Davis said. “She was a good sport.”

As darkness approached and the hiker’s phone battery drained, Davis managed to access her screen, adjust several location settings, and retrieve her GPS coordinates using the Maps and Compass apps. He immediately relayed them to search teams in the field.

Williams credited Davis’s persistence with helping searchers reach the woman sooner.

“The searchers would have found her eventually, but we found her a lot faster because Cody figured that out,” she said.

Shortly after Davis relayed the hiker’s coordinates, their call disconnected again. By the time he reconnected over FaceTime, rescuers had located the woman.

“I called her back just as teams were approaching, and we all saw the moment the first team made contact with her while she was on FaceTime,” Davis said. “It was ultimately a cool experience.”

Rescuers helped the woman return to the trail, and Williams said she walked out with them in good spirits.

Williams urged hikers to stay with their companions, particularly when members of a group move at different speeds.

If you lose your bearings, Davis advised staying on established trails rather than heading downhill in hopes of finding a road or another path. Search teams typically check trails first, he explained, and leaving them makes it harder for rescuers to find you.

He also recommended that hikers learn how to retrieve GPS coordinates from a phone’s Maps or Compass app before heading out, so they can relay their location directly to emergency responders.

Ultimately, Williams pointed to several advantages the woman had when she lost her way. She carried a charged phone, had cell service, and answered when rescuers called.

“Often when we get called for a search, somebody doesn’t call until their phone is dying, or they’ve used their flashlight for so long that the phone is dying,” she said. Starting out with a charged phone and knowing how to share coordinates can make all the difference when a routine hike takes a wrong turn.

#8195. Follow This ‘Map of Quietude’ to the Most Silent Trails in Sweden

Taking in one of the many gorgeous views along the quiet Swedish coast (Photo: Andrea Bussell)

The invitation piqued my interest as soon as it landed in my inbox: “A beachfront cabin where you can stay for free,” it read, describing a remote spot on the Baltic coast in southwest Sweden. “The only condition? You have to stay quiet.” Surrounded by apple orchards, with the sea just out the door, this idyllic place would be available to a few lucky travelers—as long as we maintained an air of “quietude” during our respective stays.

Outfitted with sound-measuring technology to monitor noise levels inside, the unique setup of the Stay Quiet Cabin is part of a broader initiative by Visit Skåne (pronounced skaw-nuh) to combat one of Europe’s most significant environmental health issues: noise pollution. According to the European Commission, prolonged exposure to loud, chronic noise is the second largest cause of health problems contributing to cardiovascular disease, sleep disturbances, and stress-related health concerns. Spending time in naturally quiet environments can help relieve those symptoms.

Skåne is a region renowned for its restorative pastoral and seaside landscapes, unique rural culture, farm-to-table restaurants, and heritage traditions. Within it, The Map of Quietude—a list of 26 places mapped by a professional sound engineer—leads to many spots along Skåne’s 1,000+ miles of hiking trails. Each spot’s silence has been measured to ensure distinctly healing experiences.

I found that pausing in them to take in the stillness and beauty added something beyond a typical travel or hiking experience. It gave me insight into the true frequency of a place and what it offers: peace, an immersion in rejuvenating slowness, and awe. After my days in silence on the coast, I’ve rounded up some best trails where you can easily experience these locations of quietude, while also taking in interesting communities, historic sites, and some of Scandinavia’s most beautiful wildernesses. Sweden’s nature-centric way of life includes the right of public access, or allemansrätten, which allows hiking or camping almost anywhere in the countryside with the expectation that you will respect the land.

Distance: 7.5 miles Part of the Öresund Way, this loop is worth a detour from inland Skåne to discover a car-free island where people come to bike and hike. You can also get some of the region’s best cardamom buns at Hven Durum, a family-run bakery and mill.

A quick ferry will bring you to this tiny slip of seaside heaven. Walk along the coastline and through a species-rich nature reserve for sweeping views of the Öre Sound and Copenhagen skyline. Ven’s southern headland, södra udde, is a nature reserve and designated place of quietude. See an active, mid-20th-century lighthouse nearby. Or, check out the site of 16th-century Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe’s observatory.

Distance: 7.4 Miles (bonus summit extends to 11.4 miles)

Starting at the edge of the Kulla peninsula in northwest Skåne, you’ll trace roughly seven and a half miles of mostly flat shoreline south from the small fishing village Mölle. One of Sweden’s first seaside resorts at the turn of the 19th century, city dwellers came here for their nature fix. Back then, Mölle was steeped in scandal when, after long hikes, men and women began swimming together in the sea nearby, something that was unthinkable at the time.

The route explores nature reserves and gnarled pine forests and winds past beaches and historic towns. You’ll even pass remains of Kulla fälad, a vast historic pasture that served as a shared grazing land for livestock for centuries. In some places, ancient drystone walls are still visible. You’ll end in Höganäs, a globally renowned center of stoneware and ceramics production. It’s also a great place to explore a burgeoning creative community. Stop by The Hub Höganäs to experience local life, where artists sell heritage-steeped crafts, and locals gather for events. If you’re looking for a great place to eat, try Hubben, a local spot run by friendly Swedes.

To visit a place of Quietude, start in the spectacular Kullaberg Nature Reserve. From there, head to Håkull, the region’s highest peak. The summit offers panoramic views of the sea and Danish coastline. It will add about four miles to your trek.

Distance: 117 miles For over 100 miles, the Österlen Way traverses the southeast corner of Skåne. This is Sweden’s famed culinary region. It’s also where my Stay Quiet Cabin was located. Starting in the medieval town of Ystad, the Österlen Way follows the Baltic Sea coast. It passes through nature reserves, national parks, and fishing villages, with inland stretches through ancient forest.

Among other fascinating stops, you’ll pass the hilltop stone circle, Ales Stenar. This is often referred to as “Sweden’s Stonehenge” for its similarly mysterious origins. The trail has two spots of Quietude. The first is Meditationsplatsen, a circular enclosure where people come to meditate. There’s also Gislövshammar Quarry, a 19th-century limestone quarry on the coast of its namesake fishing village. This area is known for its many orchards, farms, and excellent independent shops and bakeries.

Distance: 113 miles This breathtaking route hugs the wave-swept coastline of the Öresund Strait. From north to south, it passes through historic fishing villages and dramatic landscapes. It combines previously mentioned trails and quiet spots (Håkull, Mölle to Höganäs, and Ven Island) with two additional places of Quietude. There are the historic open-air cold bathing houses Pålsjöbaden and Hilleshögs dalar valley.

Hikers pass beaches, meadows, dunes and cliffs, and enter pine forests. The trail varies in difficulty before finishing with a loop around the Falsterbonäset Peninsula. Stone Age graves, medieval castle ruins, and views of the Danish coast keep things interesting. The final legs of the trail provide ample opportunities for birdwatching. It enters nature reserves that are internationally renowned habitats for many of Northern Europe’s migratory birds.

Distance: 994 miles At just under 1,000 miles (1,600 km), the region’s Skåneleden trail is a long-distance route that traverses a vast amount of the countryside’s changeable terrain. You’ll encounter rocky coast, verdant forest, national parks, and nature reserves.  There are also historic sites like castles and stone circles.

The Skåneleden Trail is divided into seven sub-trails by geographic area. There are 148 sections (encompassing all the previously mentioned routes). Many individual sections make for great day hikes. Or, combine them for longer treks over multiple days or weeks. Several sections are near train or bus stations, making transportation easy. Basic campsites with wind shelters and bathrooms are available along the way for those seeking a longer adventure.

**You can hear 60-minute field recordings of birdsong, waves, and wind from each of the places of quietude mentioned above on Visit Skåne’s website or Spotify.

#8194. Field Tested From the High Sierra to the French Alps: Sportiva’s Newest Approach Shoe

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Hand cracks are not the ideal terrain for the TX1, but they are just too fun to pass up. (Photo: Anthony Walsh)

There are three things that make an approach shoe “high value:” its price, versatility, and durability. At $159, La Sportiva’s all-new TX1 (replacing the cult-classic TX2) is decently affordable, and was versatile enough to take testers across a range of objectives, including fifth-class ridges in the Sierras and daily crag commutes, and be worn as a slip-on between limit boulder problems. I logged dozens of scrambling pitches in my TX1s and noted no signs of premature wear along the TPU-coated polyester upper or its Vibram MegaGrip outsole.

The breathable upper and shallow dot lugs make the TX1 an excellent shoe for the fair-weather rock climber who dodges rainy forecasts and muddy approaches. Those little lugs provide just enough grip for your average walkoff, but really shine on technical, slabby approaches where surface contact is king. On the mile-long Eagle Lake Buttress Traverse (5.0), the TX1 smeared well across its opening slabs—but I wished for a taller rand while jamming hand-sized cracks.

Fit wise, all testers found the TX1 to be comfortable out of the box, thanks to a stock 4mm Ortholite Hybrid insole and a plush Air Mesh lining. (The TX1 fits a touch wider than the TX2, for those familiar.) One tester, who has a relatively narrow, low-volume foot, loved the fit of the TX1, saying its toebox felt roomy and allowed her toes “to spread and relax naturally.” My wider foot, meanwhile, had me eager to take the TX1 off after an hour-long approach. I wish this shoe came in a slightly wider last.
